entries.784696ce64499b7adea5e091dcd99561faa7d1c2: <div sID="gen26517" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="Luke.24" sID="Luke.24"/> <div eID="gen26517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26518" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26519" type="x-p"/> Our Lord Jesus went gloriously down to death, in spite of the malice of his enemies, who did all they could to make his death ignominious; but he rose again more gloriously, of which we have an account in this chapter; and the proofs and evidences of Christ's resurrection are more fully related by this evangelist than they were by Matthew and Mark. Here is, I. Assurance given by two angels, to the woman who visited the sepulchre, that the Lord Jesus was risen from the dead, according to his own word, to which the angels refer them (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.1-Luke.24.7">ver. 1-7</reference>), and the report of this to the apostles, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.8-Luke.24.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. II. The visit which Peter made to the sepulchre, and his discoveries there, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.12">ver. 12</reference>. III. Christ's conference with the two disciples that were going to Emmaus, and his making himself known to them, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.13-Luke.24.35">ver. 13-35</reference>. IV. His appearing to the eleven disciples themselves, the same day at evening, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.39-Luke.24.46">ver. 36-49</reference>. V. The farewell he gave them, his ascension into heaven, and the joy and praise of his disciples whom he left behind, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.50-Luke.24.53">ver. 50-53</reference>.
entries.c78cb49e6fcdf79c5e2f8f09b10ab209e6445490: <div eID="gen26519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26518" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Resurrection.</title> <div sID="gen26520" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now upon the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the week, very early in the morning, they came unto the sepulchre, bringing the spices which they had prepared, and certain <hi type="italic">others</hi> with them. <hi type="super">2</hi> And they found the stone rolled away from the sepulchre. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they entered in, and found not the body of the Lord Jesus. <hi type="super">4</hi> And it came to pass, as they were much perplexed thereabout, behold, two men stood by them in shining garments: <hi type="super">5</hi> And as they were afraid, and bowed down <hi type="italic">their</hi> faces to the earth, they said unto them, Why seek ye the living among the dead? <hi type="super">6</hi> He is not here, but is risen: remember how he spake unto you when he was yet in Galilee, <hi type="super">7</hi> Saying, The Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again. <hi type="super">8</hi> And they remembered his words, <hi type="super">9</hi> And returned from the sepulchre, and told all these things unto the eleven, and to all the rest. <hi type="super">10</hi> It was Mary Magdalene, and Joanna, and Mary <hi type="italic">the mother</hi> of James, and other <hi type="italic">women that were</hi> with them, which told these things unto the apostles. <hi type="super">11</hi> And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then arose Peter, and ran unto the sepulchre; and stooping down, he beheld the linen clothes laid by themselves, and departed, wondering in himself at that which was come to pass. <div eID="gen26520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26521" type="x-p"/> The manner of the re-uniting of Christ's soul and body in his resurrection is a mystery, one of the <hi type="italic">secret things</hi> that <hi type="italic">belong not to us;</hi> but the <hi type="italic">infallible proofs</hi> of his resurrection, that he did indeed rise from the dead, and was thereby proved to be the Son of God, are <hi type="italic">things revealed, which belong to us and to our children.</hi> Some of them we have here in these verses, which relate the same story for substance that we had in Matthew and Mark. <div eID="gen26521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26522" type="x-p"/> I. We have here the affection and respect which the good women that had followed Christ showed to him, after he was dead and buried, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.1">v. 1</reference>. As soon as ever they could, after the sabbath was over, they <hi type="italic">came to the sepulchre,</hi> to embalm his body, not to take it out of the linen in which Joseph had wrapped it, but to anoint the head and face, and perhaps the wounded hands and feet, and to scatter sweet spices upon and about the body; as it is usual with us to strew flowers about the dead bodies and graves of our friends, only to show our good-will towards the taking off the deformity of death if we could, and to make them somewhat the less loathsome to those that are about them. The zeal of these good women for Christ did continue. The spices which they had prepared the evening before the sabbath, at a great expense, they did not, upon second thoughts, when they had slept upon it, dispose of otherwise, suggesting, <hi type="italic">To what purpose is this waste?</hi> but they brought them to the sepulchre on the morning after the sabbath, early, very early. It is a rule of charity, <hi type="italic">Every man, according as he purposes in his heart, so let him give,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">2 Cor. ix. 7</reference>. What is prepared for Christ, let it be used for him. Notice is taken of the names of these women, <hi type="italic">Mary Magdalene,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Joanna,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mary</hi> the mother of James; grave matronly women, it should seem, they were. Notice is also taken of certain others with them, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.1">v. 1</reference>, and again, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.10">v. 10</reference>. These, who had not joined in preparing the spices, would yet go along with them to the sepulchre; as if the number of Christ's friends increased when he was dead, <reference osisRef="John.12.24">John xii. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.12.32">32</reference>. The daughters of Jerusalem, when they saw how inquisitive the souse was after her Beloved, were desirous to seek him with her (<reference osisRef="Song.6.1">Cant. vi. 1</reference>), so were these <hi type="italic">other women.</hi> The zeal of some provokes others. <div eID="gen26522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26523" type="x-p"/> II. The surprise they were in, when they found the stone rolled away and the grave empty (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.2-Luke.24.3">v. 2, 3</reference>); they were <hi type="italic">much perplexed</hi> at that (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.4">v. 4</reference>) which they had much reason to rejoice in, that <hi type="italic">the stone was rolled away from the sepulchre</hi> (by which it appeared that he had a legal discharge, and leave to come out), and that they <hi type="italic">found not the body of the Lord Jesus,</hi> by which it appeared that he had made us of his discharge and was come out. Note, Good Christians often perplex themselves about that with which they should comfort and encourage themselves. <div eID="gen26523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26524" type="x-p"/> III. The plain account which they had of Christ's resurrection from two angels, who appeared to them <hi type="italic">in shining garments,</hi> not only white, but bright, and casting a lustre about them. They first saw <hi type="italic">one</hi> angel without the sepulchre, who presently <hi type="italic">went in,</hi> and sat with another angel in the sepulchre, <hi type="italic">one at the head and the other at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain;</hi> so the evangelists may be reconciled. The women, when they saw the angels, <hi type="italic">were afraid</hi> lest they had some ill news for them; but, instead of enquiring of them, they <hi type="italic">bowed down their faces to the earth,</hi> to look for their dear Master in the grave. They would rather find him in his <hi type="italic">grave-clothes</hi> than angels themselves in their <hi type="italic">shining garments.</hi> A dying Jesus has more beauty in the eyes of a believer than angels themselves. These women, like the spouse, when found by the watchman (and angels are called <hi type="italic">watchers</hi>), enter not into any other conversation with them than this, <hi type="italic">Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?</hi> Now here, 1. They upbraid the women with the absurdity of the search they were making: <hi type="italic">Why seek ye the living among the dead?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.5">v. 5</reference>. Witness is hereby given to Christ that he is <hi type="italic">living,</hi> of him <hi type="italic">it is witnessed that he liveth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.8">Heb. vii. 8</reference>), and it is the comfort of all the saints, <hi type="italic">I know that my Redeemer liveth;</hi> for because he lives we shall live also. But a reproof is given to those that look for him <hi type="italic">among the dead,</hi>—that look for him among the dead heroes that the Gentiles worshipped, as if he were but like one of them,—that look for him in an image, or a crucifix, the work of men's hands, or among unwritten tradition and the inventions of men; and indeed all they that expect happiness and satisfaction in the creature, or perfection in this imperfect state, may be said to <hi type="italic">seek the living among the dead.</hi> 2. They assure them that he is risen from the dead (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He is not here, but is risen,</hi> is risen by his own power; he has quitted his grace, to return no more to it." These angels were competent witnesses, for they had been sent express from heaven with orders for his discharge. And we are sure that their record is true; they durst not tell a lie. 3. They refer them to his own words: <hi type="italic">Remember what he spoke to you, when he was yet in Galilee.</hi> If they had duly believed and observed the prediction of it, they would easily have believed the thing itself when it came to pass; and therefore, that the tidings might not be such a surprise to them and they seemed to be, the angels repeat to them what Christ had often said in their hearing, <hi type="italic">The Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men,</hi> and though it was done by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, yet they that did it were not the less <hi type="italic">sinful</hi> for doing it. He told them that he <hi type="italic">must be crucified.</hi> Surely they could not forget that which they had with so much concern seen fulfilled; and would not this bring to their mind that which always followed, <hi type="italic">The third day he shall rise again?</hi> Observe, These angels from heaven bring not any <hi type="italic">new gospel,</hi> but put them in mind, as the angels of the churches do, of the sayings of Christ, and teach them how to improve and apply them. <div eID="gen26524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26525" type="x-p"/> IV. Their satisfaction in this account, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.8">v. 8</reference>. The women seemed to acquiesce; they <hi type="italic">remembered his words,</hi> when they were thus put in mind of them, and thence concluded that if he was risen it was not more than they had reason to expect; and now they were ashamed of the preparations they had made to embalm on the third day <hi type="italic">him</hi> who had often said that he would on the third day rise again. Note, A seasonable remembrance of the words of Christ will help us to a right understanding of his providence. <div eID="gen26525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26526" type="x-p"/> V. The report they brought of this to the apostles: <hi type="italic">They returned from the sepulchre, and told all these things to the eleven, and to all the rest</hi> of Christ's disciples, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.9">v. 9</reference>. It does not appear that they were together in a body; they were <hi type="italic">scattered every one to his own,</hi> perhaps scarcely two or three of them together in the same lodgings, but one went to some of them and another to others of them, so that in a little time, that morning, they all had notice of it. But we are told (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.11">v. 11</reference>) how the report was received: <hi type="italic">Their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not.</hi> They thought it was only the fancy of the women, and imputed it to the power of imagination; for they also had forgotten Christ's words, and wanted to be put in mind of them, not only what he had said to them in Galilee some time ago, but what he had said very lately, in the night wherein he was betrayed: <hi type="italic">Again a little while, and ye shall see me. I will see you again.</hi> One cannot but be amazed at the stupidity of these disciples,—who had themselves so often professed that they believed Christ to be the Son of God and the true Messiah, had been so often told that he must die and rise again, and then enter into his glory, had seen him more than once raise the dead,—that they should be so backward to believe in his raising himself. Surely it would seem the less strange to them, when hereafter this complaint would justly be taken up <hi type="italic">by them,</hi> to remember that there was a time when it might justly have been taken up against them, <hi type="italic">Who hath believed our report?</hi> <div eID="gen26526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26527" type="x-p"/> VI. The enquiry which Peter made hereupon, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.12">v. 12</reference>. It was Mary Magdalene that brought the report to him, as appears, <reference osisRef="John.20.1-John.20.2">John xx. 1, 2</reference>, where this story of his running to the sepulchre is more particularly related. 1. Peter hastened to the sepulchre upon the report, perhaps ashamed of himself, to think that Mary Magdalene should have been there before him; and yet, perhaps, he had not been so ready to go thither now if the women had not told him, among other things, that <hi type="italic">the watch was fled.</hi> Many that are <hi type="italic">swift-footed</hi> enough when there is no danger are but <hi type="italic">cow-hearted</hi> when there is. Peter now <hi type="italic">ran to the sepulchre,</hi> who but the other day <hi type="italic">ran from his Master.</hi> 2. He looked into the sepulchre, and took notice how orderly the linen clothes in which Christ was wrapped were taken off, and folded up, and laid by themselves, but the body gone. He was very particular in making his observations, as if he would rather credit his own eyes than the testimony of the angels. 3. He went away, as he thought, not much the wiser, <hi type="italic">wondering in himself at that which was come to pass.</hi> Had he remembered the words of Christ, even this was enough to satisfy him that he was risen from the dead; but, having forgotten them, he is only amazed with the thing, and knows not what to make of it. There is many a thing puzzling and perplexing to us which would be both plain and profitable if we did but rightly understand the words of Christ, and had them ready to us.
entries.d341cf2ba4956ca004f9cb27d71ad15a4cd128e8: <div eID="gen26527" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Disciples Going to Emmaus.</title> <div sID="gen26528" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And, behold, two of them went that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was from Jerusalem <hi type="italic">about</hi> threescore furlongs. <hi type="super">14</hi> And they talked together of all these things which had happened. <hi type="super">15</hi> And it came to pass, that, while they communed <hi type="italic">together</hi> and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them. <hi type="super">16</hi> But their eyes were holden that they should not know him. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he said unto them, What manner of communications <hi type="italic">are</hi> these that ye have one to another, as ye walk, and are sad? <hi type="super">18</hi> And the one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering said unto him, Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem, and hast not known the things which are come to pass there in these days? <hi type="super">19</hi> And he said unto them, What things? And they said unto him, Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, which was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people: <hi type="super">20</hi> And how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him to be condemned to death, and have crucified him. <hi type="super">21</hi> But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel: and beside all this, to day is the third day since these things were done. <hi type="super">22</hi> Yea, and certain women also of our company made us astonished, which were early at the sepulchre; 23 And when they found not his body, they came, saying, that they had also seen a vision of angels, which said that he was alive. <hi type="super">24</hi> And certain of them which were with us went to the sepulchre, and found <hi type="italic">it</hi> even so as the women had said: but him they saw not. <hi type="super">25</hi> Then he said unto them, O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken: <hi type="super">26</hi> Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory? <hi type="super">27</hi> And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. <hi type="super">28</hi> And they drew nigh unto the village, whither they went: and he made as though he would have gone further. <hi type="super">29</hi> But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them. <hi type="super">30</hi> And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and brake, and gave to them. <hi type="super">31</hi> And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight. <hi type="super">32</hi> And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures? <hi type="super">33</hi> And they rose up the same hour, and returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and them that were with them, <hi type="super">34</hi> Saying, The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Simon. <hi type="super">35</hi> And they told what things <hi type="italic">were done</hi> in the way, and how he was known of them in breaking of bread. <div eID="gen26528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26529" type="x-p"/> This appearance of Christ to the <hi type="italic">two disciples</hi> going to Emmaus was mentioned, and but just mentioned, before (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.12">Mark xvi. 12</reference>); here it is largely related. It happened the same day that Christ rose, the first day of the new world that rose with him. One of these two disciples was <hi type="italic">Cleopas</hi> or <hi type="italic">Alpheus,</hi> said by the ancients to be the brother of Joseph, Christ's supposed father; who the other was is not certain. Some think it was Peter; it should seem indeed that Christ did appear particularly to Peter that day, which the eleven spoke of among themselves (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.34">v. 34</reference>), and Paul mentions, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.5">1 Cor. xv. 5</reference>. But it could not be Peter that was one of the <hi type="italic">two,</hi> for he was one of the <hi type="italic">eleven</hi> to whom the <hi type="italic">two</hi> returned; and, besides, we know Peter so well as to think that if he had been one of the two he would have been the <hi type="italic">chief speaker,</hi> and not Cleopas. It was one of those that were associated with the eleven, mentioned <reference osisRef="Luke.24.9">v. 9</reference>. Now in this passage of story we may observe, <div eID="gen26529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26530" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">walk</hi> and <hi type="italic">talk</hi> of these two disciples: <hi type="italic">They went to a village called Emmaus,</hi> which is reckoned to be about two hours' walk from Jerusalem; it is here said to be about sixty furlongs, seven measured miles, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.13">v. 13</reference>. Whether they went thither upon business, or to see some friend, does not appear. I suspect that they were going homewards to Galilee, with an intention not to enquire more after this Jesus; that they were meditating a retreat, and stole away from their company without asking leave or taking leave; for the accounts brought them that morning of their Master's resurrection seemed to them <hi type="italic">as idle tales;</hi> and, if so, no wonder that they began to think of making the best of their way home. But as they travelled they <hi type="italic">talked together of all those things which had happened,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.14">v. 14</reference>. They had not courage to <hi type="italic">confer</hi> of these things, and <hi type="italic">consult</hi> what was to be done in the present juncture at Jerusalem, for fear of the Jews; but, when they were got out of the hearing of the Jews, they could talk it over with more freedom. They <hi type="italic">talked over these things,</hi> reasoning with themselves concerning the probabilities of Christ's resurrection; for, according as these appeared, they would either go forward or return back to Jerusalem. Note, It well becomes the disciples of Christ, when they are together, to talk of his death and resurrection; thus they may improve one another's knowledge, refresh one another's memory, and stir up one another's devout affections. <div eID="gen26530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26531" type="x-p"/> II. The good company they met with upon the road, when Jesus himself came, and joined himself to them (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">They communed together, and reasoned,</hi> and perhaps were warm at the argument, one hoping that their Master was risen, and would set up his kingdom, the other despairing. <hi type="italic">Jesus himself drew near,</hi> as a stranger who, seeing them travel the same way that he <hi type="italic">went,</hi> told them that he should be <hi type="italic">glad of their company.</hi> We may observe it, for our encouragement to keep up Christian conference and edifying discourse among us, that where but two together are well employed in work of that kind Christ will come to them, and make a third. When they that fear the Lord <hi type="italic">speak one to another</hi> the Lord <hi type="italic">hearkens and hears,</hi> and is with them of a truth; so that two thus twisted in faith and love become a <hi type="italic">threefold cord, not easily broken,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.12">Eccl. iv. 12</reference>. They in their communings and reasonings together were searching for Christ, comparing notes concerning him, that they might come to more knowledge of him; and now Christ comes to them. Note, They who seek Christ shall find him: he will manifest himself to those that enquire after him, and give knowledge to those who use the helps for knowledge which they have. When the spouse enquired of the watchman concerning her beloved, <hi type="italic">it was but a little that she passed from them, but she found him.</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.3.4">Cant. iii. 4</reference>. But, though they had Christ with them, they were not at first aware of it (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their eyes were held, that they should not know him.</hi> It should seem, there were both an alteration of the <hi type="italic">object</hi> (for it is said in Mark that now <hi type="italic">he appeared in another form</hi>) and a restraint upon the organ (for here it is said that <hi type="italic">their eyes were held</hi> by a divine power); or, as some think, there was a confusion in the <hi type="italic">medium;</hi> the air was so disposed that they could not discern who it was. No matter <hi type="italic">how</hi> it was, but <hi type="italic">so</hi> it was they did not <hi type="italic">know him,</hi> Christ so ordering it that they might the more freely discourse with him and he with them, and that it might appear that his word, and the influence of it, did not depend upon his bodily presence, which the disciples had too much doted upon, and must be weaned from; but he could teach them, and warm their hearts, by others, who should have his spiritual presence with them, and should have his grace going along with them unseen. <div eID="gen26531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26532" type="x-p"/> III. The conference that was between Christ and them, when he knew them, and they knew not him. Now Christ and his disciples, as is usual when friends meet incognito, or in a disguise, are here crossing questions. <div eID="gen26532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26533" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ's first question to them is concerning <hi type="italic">their</hi> present <hi type="italic">sadness,</hi> which plainly appeared in their countenances: <hi type="italic">What manner of communications are those that you have one with another as you walk, and are sad?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.17">v. 17</reference>. It is a very kind and friendly enquiry. Observe, <div eID="gen26533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26534" type="x-p"/> (1.) They were <hi type="italic">sad;</hi> it appeared to a stranger that they were so. [1.] They had lost their dear Master, and were, in their own apprehensions, quite disappointed in their expectations from him. They had given up the cause, and knew not what course to take to retrieve it. Note, Christ's disciples have reason to be sad when he withdraws from them, to <hi type="italic">fast</hi> when the <hi type="italic">Bridegroom</hi> is taken from them. [2.] Though he was risen from the dead, yet either they did not know it or did not believe it, and so they were still in sorrow. Note, Christ's disciples are often sad and sorrowful even when they have reason to rejoice, but through the weakness of their faith they cannot take the comfort that is offered to them. [3.] Being sad, they had <hi type="italic">communications one with another</hi> concerning Christ. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It becomes Christians to talk of Christ. Were our hearts as full of him, and of what he has done and suffered for us, as they should be, <hi type="italic">out of the abundance of the heart the mouth would speak,</hi> not only of God and his providence, but of Christ and his grace and love. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Good company and good converse are an excellent antidote against prevailing melancholy. When Christ's disciples were sad they did not each one get by himself, but continued as he sent them out, two and two, for two are better than one, especially in times of sorrow. Giving <hi type="italic">vent</hi> to the grief may perhaps give <hi type="italic">ease</hi> to the grieved; and by talking it over we may talk ourselves or our friends may talk us into a better frame. Joint mourners should be mutual comforters; comforts sometimes come best from such. <div eID="gen26534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26535" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ came up to them, and enquired into the matter of their talk, and the cause of their grief: <hi type="italic">What manner of communications are these?</hi> Though Christ had now entered into his state of exaltation, yet he continued tender of his disciples, and concerned for their comfort. He speaks as one troubled to see their melancholy: <hi type="italic">Wherefore look ye so sadly to-day?</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.40.7">Gen. xl. 7</reference>. Note, Our Lord Jesus takes notice of the sorrow and sadness of his disciples, and is afflicted in their afflictions. Christ has hereby taught us, [1.] To be <hi type="italic">conversable.</hi> Christ here fell into discourse with two grave serious persons, though he was a stranger to them and they knew him not, and they readily embraced him. It does not become Christians to be morose and shy, but to take pleasure in good society. [2.] We are hereby taught to be <hi type="italic">compassionate.</hi> When we see our friends in sorrow and sadness, we should, like Christ here, take cognizance of their grief, and give them the best counsel and comfort we can: <hi type="italic">Weep with them that weep.</hi> <div eID="gen26535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26536" type="x-p"/> 2. In answer to this, they put a question to him concerning <hi type="italic">his strangeness. Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem, and hast not known the things that are come to pass there in these days?</hi> Observe, (1.) Cleopas gave him a civil answer. He does not rudely ask him. "As for what we are talking of, what is that to you?" and bid him go about his business. Note, We ought to be civil to those who are civil to us, and to conduct ourselves obligingly to all, both in word and deed. It was a dangerous time now with Christ's disciples; yet he was not jealous of this stranger, that he had any design upon them, to inform against them, or bring them into trouble. Charity is not forward to <hi type="italic">think evil,</hi> no, not of strangers. (2.) He is full of Christ himself and of his death and sufferings, and wonders that every body else is not so too: "What! art thou such a stranger in Jerusalem as not to know what has been done to our Master there?" Note, Those are strangers indeed in Jerusalem that know not of the death and sufferings of Christ. What! are they <hi type="italic">daughters of Jerusalem,</hi> and yet so little acquainted with Christ as to ask, <hi type="italic">What is thy beloved more than another beloved?</hi> (3.) He is very willing to inform this stranger concerning Christ, and to draw on further discourse with him upon this subject. He would not have any one that had the face of a man to be ignorant of Christ. Note, Those who have themselves the knowledge of Christ crucified should do what they can to spread that knowledge, and lead others into an acquaintance with him. And it is observable that these disciples, who were so forward to instruct the stranger, were instructed by him; for to him that has, and uses what he has, shall be given. (4.) It appears, by what Cleopas says, that the death of Christ made a great noise in Jerusalem, so that it could not be imagined that any man should be such a stranger in the city as not to know of it; it was all the talk of the town, and discoursed of in all companies. Thus the matter of fact came to be universally <hi type="italic">known,</hi> which, after the pouring out of the Spirit, was to be <hi type="italic">explained.</hi> <div eID="gen26536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26537" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ, by way of reply, asked concerning <hi type="italic">their knowledge</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">He said unto them, What things?</hi> thus making himself yet more a stranger. Observe, (1.) Jesus Christ made light of his own sufferings, in comparison with the joy set before him, which was the recompence of it. Now that he was entering upon his glory, see with what unconcernedness he looks back upon his sufferings: <hi type="italic">What things?</hi> He had reason to know what things; for to him they were bitter things, and heavy things, and yet he asks, <hi type="italic">What things?</hi> The sorrow was forgotten, for joy that the man-child of our salvation was born. He took pleasure in infirmities for our sakes, to teach us to do so for his sake. (2.) Those whom Christ will teach he will first examine how far they have learned; they must tell him <hi type="italic">what things</hi> they know, and then he will tell them what was the meaning of these things. and lead them into the mystery of them. <div eID="gen26537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26538" type="x-p"/> 4. They, hereupon, gave him a particular account concerning Christ, and the present posture of his affairs. Observe the story they tell, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.19">v. 19</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen26538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26539" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a summary of Christ's <hi type="italic">life</hi> and <hi type="italic">character.</hi> The <hi type="italic">things</hi> they are full of are concerning <hi type="italic">Jesus of Nazareth</hi> (so he was commonly called), who <hi type="italic">was a prophet,</hi> a teacher come from God. He preached a true and excellent doctrine, which had manifestly its rise from heaven, and its tendency towards heaven. He confirmed it by many glorious miracles, miracles of mercy, so that he was <hi type="italic">mighty in deed and word before God and all the people;</hi> that is, he was both a great favourite of heaven and a great blessing to this earth. He was, and appeared to be, greatly beloved of God, and much the darling of his people. He had great acceptance with God, and a great reputation in the country. Many are <hi type="italic">great before all the people,</hi> and are caressed by them, who are not so <hi type="italic">before God,</hi> as the scribes and Pharisees; but Christ was mighty both in his <hi type="italic">doctrine</hi> and in his <hi type="italic">doings, before God and all the people.</hi> Those were strangers in Jerusalem that did not know this. <div eID="gen26539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26540" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is a modest narrative of his sufferings and death, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.20">v. 20</reference>. "Though he was so dear both to God and man, yet the <hi type="italic">chief priests and our rulers,</hi> in contempt of both, <hi type="italic">delivered him</hi> to the Roman power, <hi type="italic">to be condemned to death,</hi> and <hi type="italic">they have crucified him.</hi>" It is strange that they did not aggravate the matter more, and lay a greater load upon those that had been guilty of crucifying Christ; but perhaps because they spoke to one that was a stranger they thought it prudent to avoid all reflections upon the chief priests and their rulers, how just soever. <div eID="gen26540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26541" type="x-p"/> (3.) Here is an intimation of their disappointment in him, as the reason of their sadness: "<hi type="italic">We trusted that it had been he who should have redeemed Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.21">v. 21</reference>. We are of those who not only looked upon him to be a prophet, like Moses, but, like him, a redeemer too." He was depended upon, and great things expected from him, by them that <hi type="italic">looked for redemption,</hi> and in it for the consolation of Israel. Now, if <hi type="italic">hope deferred makes the heart sick,</hi> hope disappointed, especially such a hope, kills the heart. But see how they made that the ground of their despair which if they had understood it aright was the surest ground of their hope, and that was the dying of the Lord Jesus: <hi type="italic">We trusted</hi> (say they) <hi type="italic">that it had been he that should have redeemed Israel.</hi> And is it not he that doth redeem Israel? Nay, is he not by his death paying the price of their redemption? Was it not necessary, in order to his saving Israel from their sins, that he should suffer? Sop that now, since that most difficult part of his undertaking was got over, they had more reason than ever to <hi type="italic">trust</hi> that <hi type="italic">this was he that should deliver Israel;</hi> yet now they are ready to give up the cause. <div eID="gen26541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26542" type="x-p"/> (4.) Here is an account of their present amazement with reference to his resurrection. [1.] "<hi type="italic">This is the third day</hi> since he was crucified and died, and that was the day when it was expected, if ever, that he should rise again, and rise in glory and outward pomp, and show himself as publicly in honour as he had been shown three days before in disgrace; but we see no sign of it; nothing appears, as we expected, to the conviction and confusion of his prosecutors, and the consolation of his disciples, but all is silent." [2.] They own that there was a report among them that he was risen, but they seem to speak of it very slightly, and as what they gave no credit at all to (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.22-Luke.24.23">v. 22, 23</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Certain women also of our company made us astonished</hi> (and that was all), who were <hi type="italic">early at the sepulchre,</hi> and found the body gone, and they said that they had <hi type="italic">seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive;</hi> but we are ready to think it was only their fancy, and no real thing, for angels would have been sent to the apostles, not to the women, and women are easily imposed upon." [3.] They acknowledge that some of the apostles had visited the sepulchre, and found it empty, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.24">v. 24</reference>. "But <hi type="italic">him they saw not,</hi> and therefore we have reason to fear that he <hi type="italic">is not risen,</hi> for, if he be, surely he would have <hi type="italic">shown himself</hi> to them; so that, upon the whole matter, we have no great reason to think that he is risen, and therefore have no expectations from him now; our hopes were all nailed to his cross, and buried in his grave." <div eID="gen26542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26543" type="x-p"/> (5.) Our Lord Jesus, though not known by face to them, makes himself known to them by his word. <div eID="gen26543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26544" type="x-p"/> [1.] He reproves them for their incogitancy, and the weakness of their faith in the scriptures of the Old Testament: <hi type="italic">O fools, and slow of heart to believe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.25">v. 25</reference>. When Christ forbade us to say to our brother, <hi type="italic">Thou fool,</hi> it was intended to restrain us from giving unreasonable reproaches, not from giving just reproofs. Christ called them <hi type="italic">fools,</hi> not as it signifies <hi type="italic">wicked men,</hi> in which sense he forbade it to us, but as it signifies <hi type="italic">weak men.</hi> He might call them <hi type="italic">fools,</hi> for he <hi type="italic">knows our foolishness,</hi> the foolishness that is bound in our hearts. Those are fools that act against their own interest; so they did who would not admit the evidence given them that their Master was risen, but put away the comfort of it. That which is condemned in them as their <hi type="italic">foolishness</hi> is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Their <hi type="italic">slowness to believe.</hi> Believers are branded as fools by atheists, and infidels, and free-thinkers, and their most holy faith is censured as a fond credulity; but Christ tells us that those are <hi type="italic">fools</hi> who are <hi type="italic">slow of heart to believe,</hi> and are kept from it by prejudices never impartially examined. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Their slowness to believe <hi type="italic">the writings of the prophets.</hi> He does not so much blame them for their slowness to believe the testimony of the women and of the angels, but for that which was the cause thereof, their <hi type="italic">slowness to believe</hi> the prophets; for, if they had given the prophets of the Old Testament their due weight and consideration, they would have been as sure of Christ's <hi type="italic">rising from the dead</hi> that morning (being the third day after his death) as they were of the <hi type="italic">rising of the sun;</hi> for the <hi type="italic">series</hi> and <hi type="italic">succession</hi> of events as settled by <hi type="italic">prophecy</hi> are no less certain and inviolable than as settled by <hi type="italic">providence.</hi> Were we but more <hi type="italic">conversant</hi> with the scripture, and the divine counsels as far as they are made known in the scripture, we should not be subject to such perplexities as we often <hi type="italic">entangle</hi> ourselves in. <div eID="gen26544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26545" type="x-p"/> [2.] He shows them that the sufferings of Christ, which were such a stumbling-block to them, and made them unapt to believe his glory, were really the appointed way to his glory, and he could not go to it any other way (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.26">v. 26</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Ought not the Christ</hi> (the Messiah) to <hi type="italic">have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?</hi> Was it not decreed, and was not that decree <hi type="italic">declared,</hi> that the promised Messiah must first suffer and then reign, that he must go by his cross to his crown?" Had they never read the fifty-third of Isaiah and the ninth of Daniel, where the prophets speak so very plainly of the <hi type="italic">sufferings of Christ</hi> and the <hi type="italic">glory that should follow?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>. The cross of Christ was that to which they could not reconcile themselves; now here he shows them two things which take off the offence of the cross:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the Messiah <hi type="italic">ought to suffer</hi> these things; and therefore his sufferings were not only no objection against his being the Messiah, but really a proof of it, as the afflictions of the saints are an evidence of their sonship; and they were so far from ruining their expectations that really they were the foundation of their hopes. He could not have been a <hi type="italic">Saviour,</hi> if he had not been a <hi type="italic">sufferer.</hi> Christ's undertaking our salvation was voluntary; but, having undertaken it, it was necessary that he should suffer and die. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That, when he had suffered these things, he should <hi type="italic">enter into his glory,</hi> which he did at his resurrection; that was his first step upward. Observe, It is called <hi type="italic">his</hi> glory, because he was <hi type="italic">duly entitled</hi> to it, and it was the glory he had before the world was; he <hi type="italic">ought</hi> to enter into it, for in that, as well as in his sufferings, the scripture must be fulfilled. He <hi type="italic">ought</hi> to suffer first, and then to enter into his glory; and thus the <hi type="italic">reproach</hi> of the cross is for ever <hi type="italic">rolled away,</hi> and we are directed to expect the crown of <hi type="italic">thorns</hi> and then that of <hi type="italic">glory.</hi> <div eID="gen26545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26546" type="x-p"/> [3.] He expounded to them the scriptures of the Old Testament, which spoke of the Messiah, and showed them how they were fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth, and now can tell them more concerning him than they could before tell him (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Beginning at Moses,</hi> the first inspired writer of the Old Testament, he went in order through <hi type="italic">all the prophets,</hi> and <hi type="italic">expounded to them the things concerning himself,</hi> showing that the sufferings he had now gone through were so far from defeating the prophecies of the scripture concerning him that they were the accomplishment of them. He began at Moses, who recorded the first promise, in which it was plainly foretold that the Messiah should have his <hi type="italic">heel bruised,</hi> but that by it the serpent's head should be incurably broken. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There are things dispersed throughout <hi type="italic">all the scriptures</hi> concerning Christ, which it is of great advantage to have <hi type="italic">collected</hi> and <hi type="italic">put together.</hi> You cannot go far in any part of scripture but you meet with something that has reference to Christ, some prophecy, some promise, some prayer, some type or other; for he is the true <hi type="italic">treasure his in the field</hi> of the Old Testament. A golden thread of gospel grace runs through the whole web of the Old Testament. There is an <hi type="italic">eye</hi> of that <hi type="italic">white</hi> to be discerned in every place. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The things concerning Christ need to be <hi type="italic">expounded.</hi> The eunuch, though a scholar, would not pretend to understand them, <hi type="italic">except some man should guide him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.31">Acts viii. 31</reference>); for they were delivered darkly, according to that dispensation: but now that the veil is taken away the New Testament expounds the Old. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Jesus Christ is himself the best expositor of scripture, particularly the scriptures concerning himself; and even after his resurrection it was in this way that he led people into the knowledge of the mystery concerning himself; not by advancing new notions independent upon the scripture, but by showing how the scripture was fulfilled, and turning them over to the study of it. Even the Apocalypse itself is but a second part of the Old-Testament prophecies, and has continually an eye to them. <hi type="italic">If men believe not Moses and the prophets,</hi> they are incurable. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> In <hi type="italic">studying</hi> the scriptures, it is good to be <hi type="italic">methodical,</hi> and to take them in order; for the Old-Testament light shone <hi type="italic">gradually</hi> to the <hi type="italic">perfect day,</hi> and it is good to observe how <hi type="italic">at sundry times,</hi> and in <hi type="italic">divers manners</hi> (subsequent predictions improving and giving light to the preceding ones), God spoke to the fathers <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> his Son, by whom he has now <hi type="italic">spoken</hi> to us. Some begin their bible at the wrong end, who study the Revelation first; but Christ has here taught us to <hi type="italic">begin at Moses.</hi> Thus far the conference between them. <div eID="gen26546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26547" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is the discovery which Christ at length made of himself to them. One would have given a great deal for a copy of the sermon Christ preached to them by the way, of that exposition of the bible which he gave them; but it is not thought fit that we should have it, we have the substance of it in other scriptures. The disciples are so charmed with it, that they think they are come too soon to their journey's end; but so it is: <hi type="italic">They drew nigh to the village whither they went</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.28">v. 28</reference>), where, it should seem, they determined to <hi type="italic">take up</hi> for that night. And now, <div eID="gen26547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26548" type="x-p"/> 1. They courted his stay with them: <hi type="italic">He made as though he would have gone further;</hi> he did not <hi type="italic">say</hi> that he would, but he seemed to them to be going further, and did not readily turn into their friend's house, which it would not be decent for a stranger to do unless he were invited. He would have gone further if they had not courted his stay; so that here was nothing like dissimulation in the case. If a stranger be <hi type="italic">shy,</hi> every one knows the meaning of it; he will not thrust himself <hi type="italic">rudely</hi> upon your house or company; but, if you make it appear that you are freely desirous of him for your guest or companion, he knows not but he may accept your invitation, and this was all that Christ did when he <hi type="italic">made as though he would have gone further.</hi> Note, Those that would have Christ dwell with them must invite him, and be importunate with him; though he is often <hi type="italic">found of those that seek him not,</hi> yet those only that <hi type="italic">seek</hi> can be sure to <hi type="italic">find;</hi> and, if he seem to <hi type="italic">draw off</hi> from us, it is but to draw out our importunity; as here, <hi type="italic">they constrained him;</hi> both of them laid hold on him, with a kind and friendly violence, saying, <hi type="italic">Abide with us.</hi> Note, Those that have experienced the pleasure and profit of communion with Christ cannot but covet more of his company, and beg of him, not only to <hi type="italic">walk with them</hi> all day, but to <hi type="italic">abide with them</hi> at night. When <hi type="italic">the day is far spent,</hi> and it is <hi type="italic">towards evening,</hi> we begin to think of retiring for our repose, and then it is proper to have our eye to Christ, and to beg of him to <hi type="italic">abide with us,</hi> to manifest himself to us and to fill our minds with good thoughts of him and good affections to him. Christ yielded to their importunity: He <hi type="italic">went in, to tarry with them.</hi> Thus ready is Christ to give further instructions and comforts to those who improve what they have received. He has promised that <hi type="italic">if any man open the door,</hi> to bid him welcome, he will <hi type="italic">come in to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Rev. iii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen26548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26549" type="x-p"/> 2. He manifested himself to them, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.30-Luke.24.31">v. 30, 31</reference>. We may suppose that he continued his discourse with them, which he began upon the road; for thou must talk of the things of God <hi type="italic">when thou sittest in the house as well as when thou walkest by the way.</hi> While supper was getting ready (which perhaps was soon done, the provision was so small and mean), it is probable that he entertained them with such communications as were <hi type="italic">good</hi> and <hi type="italic">to the use of edifying;</hi> and so likewise as they <hi type="italic">sat at meat</hi> his <hi type="italic">lips fed</hi> them. But still they little thought that it was Jesus himself that was all this while talking with them, till at length he was pleased to throw off his disguise, and then to withdraw. (1.) They began to suspect it was he, when, as they <hi type="italic">sat down to meat,</hi> he undertook the office of the Master of the feast, which he performed so like himself, and like what he used to do among his disciples, that by it they discerned him: <hi type="italic">He took bread, and blessed it,</hi> and <hi type="italic">brake, and gave to them.</hi> This he did with his usual air both of authority and affection, with the same gestures and mien, with the same expressions perhaps in craving a blessing and in giving the bread to them. This was not a <hi type="italic">miraculous</hi> meal like that of the five loaves, nor a <hi type="italic">sacramental</hi> meal like that of the eucharist, but a <hi type="italic">common</hi> meal; yet Christ here did the same as he did in those, to teach us to keep up our communion with God through Christ in common providences as well as in special ordinances, and to crave a blessing and give thanks at every meal, and to see our daily bread provided for us and broken to us by the hand of Jesus Christ, the Master, not only of the great family, but of all our families. Wherever we <hi type="italic">sit down to eat,</hi> let us set Christ at the upper end of the table, take our meat as <hi type="italic">blessed to us</hi> by him, and <hi type="italic">eat and drink</hi> to his glory, and receive contentedly and thankfully what he is pleased to <hi type="italic">carve</hi> out to us, be the fare ever so coarse and mean. We may well receive it cheerfully, if we can by faith see it coming to us <hi type="italic">from</hi> Christ's hand, and with his blessing. (2.) Presently <hi type="italic">their eyes were opened,</hi> and then they saw who it was, and <hi type="italic">knew him</hi> well enough. Whatever it was which had hitherto concealed him from them, it was now taken out of the way; the mists were scattered, the veil was taken off, and then they made no question but it was their Master. He might, for wise and holy ends, put on the shape of another, but no other could put on his; and therefore it must be he. See how Christ by his Spirit and grace makes himself known to the souls of his people. [1.] He opens the scriptures to them, for they are they which testify of him to those who <hi type="italic">search them,</hi> and search for him in them. [2.] He meets them at his table, in the ordinance of the Lord's supper, and commonly there makes further discoveries of himself to them, is <hi type="italic">known to them in the breaking of bread.</hi> But, [3.] The work is completed by the opening of the eyes of their mind, and causing the scales to fall off from them, as from Paul's in his conversion. If he that gives the revelation do not give the understanding, we are in the dark still. <div eID="gen26549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26550" type="x-p"/> 3. He immediately disappeared: <hi type="italic">He vanished out of their sight.</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Aphantos egeneto</hi></hi>—He <hi type="italic">withdrew himself</hi> from them, slipped away of a sudden, and went <hi type="italic">out of sight.</hi> Or, he <hi type="italic">became not visible by them,</hi> was made inconspicuous by them. It should seem that though Christ's body, after his resurrection, was the very <hi type="italic">same body</hi> in which he suffered and died, as appeared by the marks in it, yet it was so far changed as to become either <hi type="italic">visible</hi> or <hi type="italic">not visible</hi> as he thought fit to make it, which was a step towards its being made a <hi type="italic">glorious body.</hi> As soon as he had given his disciples one glimpse of him he was gone presently. Such short and transient views have we of Christ in this world; we see him, but in a little while lose the sight of him again. When we come to heaven the vision of him will have no interruptions. <div eID="gen26550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26551" type="x-p"/> V. Here is the reflection which these disciples made upon this conference, and the report which they made of it to their brethren at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen26551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26552" type="x-p"/> 1. The reflection they each of them made upon the influence which Christ's discourse had upon them (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">They said one to another, Did not our hearts burn within us?</hi> "I am sure mine did," saith one; "And so did mine," saith the other, "I never was so affected with any discourse in all my life." Thus do they not so much compare <hi type="italic">notes</hi> as compare <hi type="italic">hearts,</hi> in the review of the sermon Christ had preached to them. They found the preaching powerful, even when they knew not the preacher. It made things very plain and clear to them; and, which was more, brought a <hi type="italic">divine heat</hi> with a <hi type="italic">divine light</hi> into their souls, such as put their hearts into a glow, and kindled a holy fire of pious and devout affections in them. Now this they take notice of, for the confirming of their belief, that it was indeed, as at last they saw, <hi type="italic">Jesus himself</hi> that had been talking with them all along. "What fools were we, that we were not sooner aware who it was! For none but he, no word but his, could <hi type="italic">make our hearts burn within us</hi> as they did; it must be he that has the key of the heart; it could be no other." See here, (1.) What <hi type="italic">preaching</hi> is likely to <hi type="italic">do good</hi>—such as Christ's was, <hi type="italic">plain preaching,</hi> and that which is familiar and level to our capacity—<hi type="italic">he talked with us by the way;</hi> and <hi type="italic">scriptural</hi> preaching—<hi type="italic">he opened to us the scriptures,</hi> the scriptures relating to himself. Ministers should show people their religion in their bibles, and that they preach no other doctrine to them than what is there; they must show that they make that the fountain of their knowledge and the foundation of their faith. Note, The expounding of those scriptures which speak of Christ has a direct tendency to warm the hearts of his disciples, both to quicken and to comfort them. (2.) What <hi type="italic">hearing</hi> is likely to <hi type="italic">do good</hi>—that which makes the <hi type="italic">heart burn;</hi> when we are much affected with the things of God, especially with the love of Christ in dying for us, and have our hearts thereby drawn out in love to him, and drawn up in holy desires and devotions, then our hearts <hi type="italic">burn within us;</hi> when our hearts are raised and elevated, and are as the sparks which <hi type="italic">fly upwards</hi> towards God, and when they are kindled and carried out with a holy zeal and indignation against sin, both in others and in ourselves, and we are in some measure refined and purified from it by the <hi type="italic">spirit of judgment</hi> and the <hi type="italic">spirit of burning,</hi> then we may say, "Through grace our hearts are thus inflamed." <div eID="gen26552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26553" type="x-p"/> 2. The report they brought of this to their brethren at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">They rose up the same hour,</hi> so transported with joy at the discovery Christ had made of himself to them that they could not stay to make an end of their supper, but returned with all speed to Jerusalem, though it was towards evening. If they had had any thoughts of quitting their relation to Christ, this soon banished all such thoughts out of their mind, and there needed no more to send them back to his flock. It should seem that they intended at least to take up their quarters to-night at Emmaus; but now that they had seen Christ they could not rest till they had brought the good news to the disciples, both for the confirmation of their trembling faith and for the comfort of their sorrowful spirits, with the <hi type="italic">same comforts wherewith they were comforted of God.</hi> Note, It is the duty of those to whom Christ has manifested himself to let others know what he has done for their souls. When thou art converted, instructed, comforted, strengthen thy brethren. These disciples were <hi type="italic">full</hi> of this matter themselves, and must go to their brethren, to give vent to their joys, as well as to give them satisfaction that their Master was risen. Observe, (1.) How they found them, just when they came in among them, discoursing on the same subject, and relating another proof of the resurrection of Christ. They found the eleven, and those that were their usual companions, <hi type="italic">gathered together</hi> late in the night, to pray together, it may be, and to consider what was to be done in this juncture; and they found them <hi type="italic">saying</hi> among themselves (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">legontas</hi></hi> it is the saying of the <hi type="italic">eleven,</hi> not of the <hi type="italic">two,</hi> as is plain by the original), and when these two came in, they repeated to them with joy and triumph, <hi type="italic">The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Simon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.34">v. 34</reference>. That Peter had a sight of him before the rest of the disciples had appears <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.5">1 Cor. xv. 5</reference>, where it is said, <hi type="italic">He was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve.</hi> The angel having ordered the women to tell Peter of it particularly (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.7">Mark xvi. 7</reference>), for his comfort, it is highly probable that our Lord Jesus did himself presently the same day appear to Peter, though we have no particular narrative of it, to <hi type="italic">confirm the word of his messengers.</hi> This he had related to his brethren; but, observe, Peter does not here proclaim it, and boast of it, himself (he thought this did not become a penitent), but the other disciples speak of it with exultation, <hi type="italic">The Lord is risen indeed,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ontos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">really;</hi> it is now past dispute, no room is left to doubt it, for he has appeared not only to the women, but to Simon. (2.) How they seconded their evidence with an account of what they had seen (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">They told what things were done in the way.</hi> The words that were spoken by Christ to them in the way, having a wonderful effect and influence upon them, are here called the <hi type="italic">things</hi> that were <hi type="italic">done in the way;</hi> for the words that Christ speaks are not an empty sound, but <hi type="italic">they are spirit and they are life,</hi> and wondrous things are <hi type="italic">done</hi> by them, done <hi type="italic">by the way,</hi> by the by as it were, where it is not expected. They told also how he was at length <hi type="italic">known to them in the breaking of bread;</hi> then, when he was carving out blessings to them, God opened their eyes to discern who it was. Note, It would be of great use for the discovery and confirmation of truth if the disciples of Christ would compare their observations and experiences, and communicate to each other what they know and have felt in themselves.
entries.0d34faaa74a7ea780c8e784f1b0e2c96c801b654: <div eID="gen26553" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Interview with the Apostles.</title> <div sID="gen26554" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> And as they thus spake, Jesus himself stood in the midst of them, and saith unto them, Peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> unto you. <hi type="super">37</hi> But they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit. <hi type="super">38</hi> And he said unto them, Why are ye troubled? and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? <hi type="super">39</hi> Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have. 40 And when he had thus spoken, he showed them <hi type="italic">his</hi> hands and <hi type="italic">his</hi> feet. <hi type="super">41</hi> And while they yet believed not for joy, and wondered, he said unto them, Have ye here any meat? <hi type="super">42</hi> And they gave him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb. <hi type="super">43</hi> And he took <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and did eat before them. <hi type="super">44</hi> And he said unto them, These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the prophets, and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the psalms, concerning me. 45 Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures, <hi type="super">46</hi> And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day: <hi type="super">47</hi> And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. <hi type="super">48</hi> And ye are witnesses of these things. <hi type="super">49</hi> And, behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high. <div eID="gen26554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26555" type="x-p"/> Five times Christ was seen the same day that he rose: by Mary Magdalene alone in the garden (<reference osisRef="John.20.14">John xx. 14</reference>), by the women as they were going to tell the disciples (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.9">Matt. xxviii. 9</reference>), by Peter alone, by the two disciples going to Emmaus, and now at night by the eleven, of which we have an account in these verses, as also <reference osisRef="John.20.19">John xx. 19</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen26555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26556" type="x-p"/> 1. The great <hi type="italic">surprise</hi> which his appearing gave them. He came in among them very <hi type="italic">seasonably,</hi> as they were comparing notes concerning the proofs of his resurrection: <hi type="italic">As they thus spoke,</hi> and were ready perhaps to <hi type="italic">put it to the question</hi> whether the proofs produced amounted to evidence sufficient of their Master's resurrection or no, and how they should proceed, <hi type="italic">Jesus himself stood in the midst of them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">put it out of question.</hi> Note, Those who make the best use they can of their evidences for their comfort may expect further assurances, and that the <hi type="italic">Spirit of Christ</hi> will <hi type="italic">witness with their spirits</hi> (as Christ here witnessed with the disciples, and confirmed their testimony) that they are the <hi type="italic">children of God,</hi> and risen with Christ. Observe, 1. The <hi type="italic">comfort</hi> Christ spoke to them: <hi type="italic">Peace be unto you.</hi> This intimates in general that it was a kind visit which Christ now paid them, a visit of love and friendship. Though they had very unkindly deserted him in his sufferings, yet he takes the first opportunity of seeing them together; for he deals not with us as we deserve. They did not <hi type="italic">credit</hi> those who had seen him; therefore he <hi type="italic">comes himself,</hi> that they might not continue in their disconsolate incredulity. He had promised that after his resurrection he <hi type="italic">would see them in Galilee;</hi> but so desirous was he to see them, and satisfy them, that he anticipated the appointment and <hi type="italic">sees them at Jerusalem.</hi> Note, Christ is often <hi type="italic">better</hi> than his word, but never <hi type="italic">worse.</hi> Now his first word to them was, <hi type="italic">Peace be to you;</hi> not in a way of compliment, but of consolation. This was a common form of salutation among the Jews, and Christ would thus express his usual familiarity with them, though he had now entered into his state of exaltation. Many, when they are advanced, forget their old friends and take state upon them; but we see Christ as free with them as ever. Thus Christ would at the first word intimate to them that he did not come to quarrel with Peter for <hi type="italic">denying</hi> him and the rest for <hi type="italic">running away</hi> from him; no, he <hi type="italic">came peaceably,</hi> to signify to them that he had forgiven them, and was reconciled to them. 2. The <hi type="italic">fright</hi> which they put themselves into upon it (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.37">v. 37</reference>): They were <hi type="italic">terrified,</hi> supposing that <hi type="italic">they had seen a spirit,</hi> because he came in among them without any noise, and was in the midst of them ere they were aware. The word used (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.26">Matt. xiv. 26</reference>), when they said <hi type="italic">It is a spirit,</hi> is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">phantasma</hi></hi>, it is a <hi type="italic">spectre,</hi> an <hi type="italic">apparition;</hi> but the word here used is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pneuma</hi></hi>, the word that properly signifies <hi type="italic">a spirit;</hi> they supposed it to be a spirit not clothed with a real body. Though we have an alliance and correspondence with the world of spirits, and are hastening to it, yet while we are here in this world of sense and matter it is a terror to us to have a spirit so far change its own nature as to become visible to us, and conversable with us, for it is something, and bodes something, very extraordinary. <div eID="gen26556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26557" type="x-p"/> II. The great <hi type="italic">satisfaction</hi> which his discourse gave them, wherein we have, <div eID="gen26557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26558" type="x-p"/> 1. The reproof he gave them for their causeless fears: <hi type="italic">Why are you troubled, and why do</hi> frightful <hi type="italic">thoughts arise in your hearts?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.38">v. 38</reference>. Observe here, (1.) That when at any time we are <hi type="italic">troubled, thoughts</hi> are apt to <hi type="italic">rise in our hearts</hi> that do us hurt. Sometimes the <hi type="italic">trouble</hi> is the effect of the <hi type="italic">thoughts</hi> that <hi type="italic">arise in our hearts;</hi> our griefs and fears take rise from those things that are the creatures of our own fancy. Sometimes the thoughts arising in the heart are the effect of the trouble, without are fightings and then within are fears. Those that are melancholy and troubled in mind have <hi type="italic">thoughts arising in their hearts</hi> which reflect dishonour upon God, and create disquiet to themselves. <hi type="italic">I am cut off from thy sight. The Lord has forsaken and forgotten me.</hi> (2.) That many of the troublesome thoughts with which our minds are disquieted arise from our mistakes concerning Christ. They here thought that they had <hi type="italic">seen a spirit,</hi> when they saw Christ, and that put them into this fright. We forget that Christ is our <hi type="italic">elder brother,</hi> and look upon him to be at as great a distance from us as the world of spirits is from this world, and therewith terrify ourselves. When Christ is by his Spirit convincing and humbling us, when he is by his providence trying and converting us, we <hi type="italic">mistake him,</hi> as if he designed our hurt, and this troubles us. (3.) That all the troublesome thoughts which rise in our hearts at any time are known to the Lord Jesus, even at the first rise of them, and they are displeasing to him. He chid his disciples for such <hi type="italic">thoughts,</hi> to teach us to chide ourselves for them. <hi type="italic">Why art thou cast down, O my soul? Why art thou troubled?</hi> Why do <hi type="italic">thoughts arise</hi> that are neither <hi type="italic">true</hi> nor <hi type="italic">good,</hi> that have neither <hi type="italic">foundation</hi> nor <hi type="italic">fruit,</hi> but hinder our joy in God, unfit us for our duty, give advantage to Satan, and deprive us of the comforts laid up for us? <div eID="gen26558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26559" type="x-p"/> 2. The proof he gave them of his resurrection, both for the <hi type="italic">silencing</hi> of their <hi type="italic">fears</hi> by convincing them that he was <hi type="italic">not a spirit,</hi> and for the <hi type="italic">strengthening</hi> of their <hi type="italic">faith</hi> in that doctrine which they were to preach to the world by giving them full satisfaction concerning his resurrection. Two proofs he gives them:— <div eID="gen26559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26560" type="x-p"/> (1.) He shows them his body, particularly <hi type="italic">his hands and his feet.</hi> They saw that he had the shape, and features, and exact resemblance, of their Master; but is it not his ghost? "No," saith Christ, "<hi type="italic">behold my hands and my feet;</hi> you see I have <hi type="italic">hands</hi> and <hi type="italic">feet,</hi> and therefore have a <hi type="italic">true</hi> body; you see I can <hi type="italic">move</hi> these hands and feet, and therefore have a <hi type="italic">living</hi> body; and you see the marks of the nails in my hands and feet, and therefore it is <hi type="italic">my own</hi> body, the <hi type="italic">same</hi> that you saw crucified, and not a <hi type="italic">borrowed</hi> one." He lays down this principle—that a <hi type="italic">spirit has not flesh and bones;</hi> it is not compounded of gross matter, shaped into various members, and consisting of divers heterogeneous parts, as our bodies are. He does not tell us what a <hi type="italic">spirit</hi> is (it is time enough to know that when we go to the world of spirits), but what it is not: <hi type="italic">It has not flesh and bones.</hi> Now hence he infers, "<hi type="italic">It is I myself,</hi> whom you have been so intimately acquainted with, and have had such familiar conversation with; it is <hi type="italic">I myself,</hi> whom you have reason to rejoice in, and not to be afraid of." Those who <hi type="italic">know Christ</hi> aright, and know him as <hi type="italic">theirs,</hi> will have no reason to be terrified at his appearances, at his approaches. [1.] He appeals to their <hi type="italic">sight, shows</hi> them <hi type="italic">his hands</hi> and <hi type="italic">his feet,</hi> which were pierced with the nails. Christ retained the marks of them in his glorified body, that they might be proofs that it was he himself; and he was willing that they should be <hi type="italic">seen.</hi> He afterwards showed them to Thomas, for he is not ashamed of his sufferings for us; little reason then have we to be ashamed of them, or of ours for him. As he showed his wounds here to his disciples, for the enforcing of his instructions to them, so he showed them to his Father, for the enforcing of his intercessions with him. He appears in heaven <hi type="italic">as a Lamb that had been slain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.6">Rev. v. 6</reference>); his <hi type="italic">blood speaks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.24">Heb. xii. 24</reference>. He makes intercession in the virtue of his satisfaction; he says to the Father, as here to the disciples, <hi type="italic">Behold my hands and my feet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.13.6-Zech.13.7">Zech. xiii. 6, 7</reference>. [2.] He appeals to their <hi type="italic">touch: Handle me, and see.</hi> He would not let Mary Magdalene touch him at that time, <reference osisRef="John.20.17">John xx. 17</reference>. But the disciples here are entrusted to do it, that they who were to preach his resurrection, and to suffer for doing so, might be themselves abundantly satisfied concerning it. He bade them <hi type="italic">handle him,</hi> that they might be convinced that he was not a <hi type="italic">spirit.</hi> If there were really no spirits, or apparitions of spirits (as by this and other instances it is plain that the disciples did believe there were), this had been a proper time for Christ to have undeceived them, by telling them there were no such things; but he seems to take it for granted that there have been and may be apparitions of spirits, else what need was there of so much pains to prove that he was not one? There were many heretics in the primitive times, atheists I rather think they were, who said that Christ had never any substantial body, but that it was a mere phantasm, which was neither really born nor truly suffered. Such wild notions as these, we are told, the Valentinians and Manichees had, and the followers of Simon Magus; they were called <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Doketai</hi></hi> and <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Phantysiastai</hi></hi>. Blessed be God, these heresies have long since been <hi type="italic">buried;</hi> and we know and are sure that Jesus Christ was no <hi type="italic">spirit</hi> or <hi type="italic">apparition,</hi> but had a true and real body, even after his resurrection. <div eID="gen26560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26561" type="x-p"/> (2.) He <hi type="italic">eats</hi> with them, to show that he had a real and true body, and that he was willing to converse freely and familiarly with his disciples, as one friend with another. Peter lays a great stress upon this (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.41">Acts x. 41</reference>): We <hi type="italic">did eat and drink with him after he rose from the dead.</hi> <div eID="gen26561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26562" type="x-p"/> [1.] When they <hi type="italic">saw his hands and his feet,</hi> yet they knew not what to say, <hi type="italic">They believed not for joy, and wondered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.41">v. 41</reference>. It was their infirmity that they <hi type="italic">believed not,</hi> that <hi type="italic">yet</hi> they believed not, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eti apistounton auton</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">they as yet being unbelievers.</hi> This very much corroborates the truth of Christ's resurrection that the disciples were so slow to believe it. Instead of stealing away his body, and saying, <hi type="italic">He is risen,</hi> when he is not, as the chief priests suggested they would do, they are ready to say again and again, <hi type="italic">He is not risen,</hi> when he is. Their being incredulous of it at first, and insisting upon the utmost proofs of it, show that when afterwards they did believe it, and venture their all upon it, it was not but upon the fullest demonstration of the thing that could be. But, though it was their infirmity, yet it was an excusable one; for it was not from any contempt of the evidence offered them that they believed not: but, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They <hi type="italic">believed not for joy,</hi> as Jacob, when he was told that Joseph was alive; they thought it too good news to be true. When the faith and hope are therefore <hi type="italic">weak</hi> because the love and desires are <hi type="italic">strong,</hi> that weak faith shall be helped, and not rejected. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They <hi type="italic">wondered;</hi> they thought it not only <hi type="italic">too good,</hi> but <hi type="italic">too great,</hi> to be true, forgetting both the scriptures and the power of God. <div eID="gen26562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26563" type="x-p"/> [2.] For their further conviction and encouragement, he <hi type="italic">called for some meat.</hi> He sat down to meat with the two disciples at Emmaus, but it is not said that he did eat with <hi type="italic">them;</hi> now, lest that should be made an objection, he here did actually <hi type="italic">eat</hi> with <hi type="italic">them</hi> and <hi type="italic">the rest,</hi> to show that his body was really and truly <hi type="italic">returned to life,</hi> though he did not eat and drink, and converse constantly, with them, as he had done (and as Lazarus did after <hi type="italic">his</hi> resurrection, who not only returned to life, but to his former state of life, and to die again), because it was not agreeable to the economy of the state he was risen to. They gave him a <hi type="italic">piece of a broiled fish, and of a honey-comb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.42">v. 42</reference>. The honey-comb, perhaps, was used as sauce to the broiled fish, for Canaan was a land <hi type="italic">flowing with honey.</hi> This was mean fare; yet, if it be the fare of the disciples, their Master will fare as they do, because in the kingdom of our Father they shall fare as he does, shall eat and drink with him in his kingdom. <div eID="gen26563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26564" type="x-p"/> 3. The <hi type="italic">insight</hi> he gave them into the word of God, which they had <hi type="italic">heard</hi> and read, by which faith in the resurrection of Christ is wrought in them, and all the difficulties are cleared. (1.)
