He refers them to the <hi type="italic">word</hi> which they had <hi type="italic">heard</hi> from him when he was with them, and puts them in mind of that as the angel had done (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.44">v. 44</reference>): <hi type="italic">These are the words which I said unto you</hi> in private, many a time, <hi type="italic">while I was yet with you.</hi> We should better <hi type="italic">understand</hi> what Christ <hi type="italic">does,</hi> if we did but better <hi type="italic">remember</hi> what he hath <hi type="italic">said,</hi> and had but the art of comparing them together. (2.) He refers them to the <hi type="italic">word</hi> they had read in the Old Testament, to which the word they had heard from him directed them: <hi type="italic">All things must be fulfilled which were written.</hi> Christ had given them this general hint for the regulating of their expectations—that whatever they found written concerning the Messiah, in the Old Testament, must be fulfilled in him, what was written concerning his sufferings as well as what was written concerning his kingdom; these God had <hi type="italic">joined together</hi> in the prediction, and it could not be thought that they should be <hi type="italic">put asunder</hi> in the event. <hi type="italic">All things</hi> must be fulfilled, even the <hi type="italic">hardest,</hi> even the <hi type="italic">heaviest,</hi> even the <hi type="italic">vinegar;</hi> he could not die till he had that, because he could not till then say, <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> The several parts of the Old Testament are here mentioned, as containing each of them things concerning Christ: <hi type="italic">The law of Moses,</hi> that is, the Pentateuch, or the <hi type="italic">five</hi> books written by Moses,—the <hi type="italic">prophets,</hi> containing not only the books that are purely prophetical, but those historical books that were written by prophetical men,—the <hi type="italic">Psalms,</hi> containing the other writings, which they called the <hi type="italic">Hagiographa.</hi> See in what various ways of writing God did of old reveal his will; but all proceeded from one and the self-same Spirit, who by them gave notice of the coming and kingdom of the Messiah; for <hi type="italic">to him bore all the prophets witness.</hi> (3.) By an immediate present work upon their minds, of which they themselves could not but be sensible, he gave them to apprehend the true intent and meaning of the Old-Testament prophecies of Christ, and to see them all fulfilled in him: <hi type="italic">Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.45">v. 45</reference>. In his discourse with the two disciples he took the veil from off the text, by <hi type="italic">opening</hi> the scriptures; here he took the veil from off the heart, <hi type="italic">by opening the mind.</hi> Observe here, [1.] That Jesus Christ by his Spirit operates on the minds of men, on the minds of all that are his. He has access to our spirits, and can immediately influence them. It is observable how he did now after his resurrection give a <hi type="italic">specimen</hi> of those two great operations of <hi type="italic">his Spirit</hi> upon the <hi type="italic">spirits of</hi> men, his enlightening the intellectual faculties with a divine light, when he opened the understandings of his disciples, and his invigorating the active powers with a divine heat, when he made their hearts burn within them. [2.] Even good men need to have their <hi type="italic">understandings opened;</hi> for though they are not <hi type="italic">darkness,</hi> as they were by nature, yet in many things they are <hi type="italic">in the dark.</hi> David prays, <hi type="italic">Open mine eyes. Give me understanding.</hi> And Paul, who knows so much of Christ, sees his need to learn more. [3.] Christ's way of working faith in the soul, and gaining the throne there, is by <hi type="italic">opening the understanding</hi> to discern the evidence of those things that are to be believed. Thus he comes into the soul by <hi type="italic">the door,</hi> while Satan, as a thief and a robber, climbs up some other way. [4.] The design of opening the understanding is <hi type="italic">that we may understand the scriptures;</hi> not that we may be <hi type="italic">wise above what is written,</hi> but that we may be <hi type="italic">wiser in what is written,</hi> and may be made <hi type="italic">wise to salvation</hi> by it. The Spirit in the word and the Spirit in the heart say the same thing. Christ's scholars never learn <hi type="italic">above their bibles</hi> in this world; but they need to be learning still more and more <hi type="italic">out of their bibles,</hi> and to grow more <hi type="italic">ready</hi> and <hi type="italic">mighty</hi> in the scriptures. That we may have right thoughts of Christ, and have our mistakes concerning him rectified, there needs no more than to be made to understand the scriptures. <div eID="gen26564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26565" type="x-p"/> 4. The instructions he gave them as <hi type="italic">apostles,</hi> who were to be employed in setting up his kingdom in the world. They expected, while their Master was with them, that they should be preferred to posts of honour, of which they thought themselves quite disappointed when he was dead. "No," saith, he, "you are now to enter upon them; <hi type="italic">you are</hi> to be <hi type="italic">witnesses of these things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.48">v. 48</reference>), to carry the notice of them to all the world; not only to <hi type="italic">report</hi> them as matter of news, but to <hi type="italic">assert</hi> them as evidence given upon the trial of the great cause that has been so long depending between God and Satan, the issue of which must be the casting down and casting out of the <hi type="italic">prince of this world.</hi> You are fully assured of these things yourselves, you are eye and ear-witnesses of them; go, and assure the world of them; and the same Spirit that has enlightened you shall go along with you for the enlightening of others." Now here they are told, <div eID="gen26565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26566" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">What they must preach.</hi> They must preach the gospel, must preach the <hi type="italic">New Testament</hi> as the full accomplishment of the <hi type="italic">Old,</hi> as the continuation and conclusion of divine revelation. They must take their bibles along with them (especially when they preached to the Jews; nay, and Peter, in his first sermon to the Gentiles, directed them to consult the prophets, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.43">Acts x. 43</reference>), and must show people how it was written of old concerning the Messiah, and the glories and graces of his kingdom, and then must tell them how, upon their certain knowledge, all this was fulfilled in the Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen26566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26567" type="x-p"/> [1.] The great <hi type="italic">gospel truth</hi> concerning the <hi type="italic">death</hi> and <hi type="italic">resurrection</hi> of Jesus Christ must be <hi type="italic">published</hi> to the children of men (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.46">v. 46</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thus it was written</hi> in the sealed book of the divine counsels from eternity, the volume of that book of the covenant of redemption; and thus it was written in the open book of the Old Testament, among the things revealed; and therefore <hi type="italic">thus it behoved Christ to suffer,</hi> for the divine counsels must be performed, and care taken that no word of God fall to the ground. "Go, and tell the world," <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "That Christ <hi type="italic">suffered,</hi> as it was written of him. Go, preach <hi type="italic">Christ crucified;</hi> be not ashamed of his cross, not ashamed of a suffering Jesus. Tell them what he suffered, and why he suffered, and how all the scriptures of the Old Testament were fulfilled in his sufferings. Tell them that it <hi type="italic">behoved him to suffer,</hi> that it was necessary to the taking away of the sin of the world, and the deliverance of mankind from death and ruin: nay, it <hi type="italic">became him</hi> to be perfected <hi type="italic">through sufferings,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">Heb. ii. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "That he rose from the dead on <hi type="italic">the third day,</hi> by which not only all the offence of the cross was rolled away, but he was declared to be the Son of God with power, and in this also the <hi type="italic">scriptures</hi> were <hi type="italic">fulfilled</hi> (see <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3-1Cor.15.4">1 Cor. xv. 3, 4</reference>); go, tell the world how often you saw him after he rose from the dead, and how intimately you conversed with him. <hi type="italic">Your eyes see</hi>" (as Joseph said to his brethren, when his discovering himself to them was as life from the dead) "<hi type="italic">that it is my mouth that speaketh unto you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.45.12">Gen. xlv. 12</reference>. Go, and tell them, then, that he that <hi type="italic">was dead is alive,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lives for evermore,</hi> and <hi type="italic">has the keys of death and the grave,</hi>" <div eID="gen26567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26568" type="x-p"/> [2.] The great <hi type="italic">gospel duty</hi> of <hi type="italic">repentance</hi> must be <hi type="italic">pressed</hi> upon the children of men. <hi type="italic">Repentance for sin</hi> must be preached in <hi type="italic">Christ's name,</hi> and by his authority, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">v. 47</reference>. <hi type="italic">All men every where</hi> must be called and <hi type="italic">commanded to repent,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.17.30">Acts xvii. 30</reference>. "Go, and tell all people that the God that made them, and the Lord that bought them, expects and requires that, immediately upon this notice given, they turn from the worship of the gods that they have made to the worship of the God that made them; and not only so, but from serving the interests of the world and the flesh; they must turn to the service of God in Christ, must mortify all sinful habits, and forsake all sinful practices. Their hearts and lives must be changed, and they must be universally renewed and reformed." <div eID="gen26568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26569" type="x-p"/> [3.] The great <hi type="italic">gospel privilege</hi> of the <hi type="italic">remission of sins</hi> must be <hi type="italic">proposed</hi> to all, and assured to all that <hi type="italic">repent,</hi> and <hi type="italic">believe the gospel.</hi> "Go, tell a guilty world, that stands convicted and condemned at God's bar, that an act of indemnity has passed the royal assent, which all that repent and believe shall have the benefit of, and not only be <hi type="italic">pardoned,</hi> but <hi type="italic">preferred</hi> by. Tell them that <hi type="italic">there is hope</hi> concerning them." <div eID="gen26569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26570" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">To whom they must preach.</hi> Whither must they carry these proposals, and how far does their commission extend? They are here told, [1.] That they must preach this <hi type="italic">among all nations.</hi> They must disperse themselves, like the sons of Noah after the flood, some one way and some another, and carry this light along with them wherever they go. The prophets had preached <hi type="italic">repentance</hi> and <hi type="italic">remission</hi> to the <hi type="italic">Jews,</hi> but the apostles must preach them to <hi type="italic">all the world.</hi> None are <hi type="italic">exempted</hi> from the obligations the gospel lays upon men to <hi type="italic">repent,</hi> nor are any <hi type="italic">excluded</hi> from those inestimable benefits which are included in the remission of sins, but those that by their unbelief and impenitency put a bar in their own door. [2.] That they must <hi type="italic">begin at Jerusalem</hi> There they must preach their first <hi type="italic">gospel sermon;</hi> there the <hi type="italic">gospel church</hi> must be first formed; there the gospel day must dawn, and thence that light shall go forth which must take hold on the ends of the earth. And why must they begin there? <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because <hi type="italic">thus it was written,</hi> and therefore it <hi type="italic">behoved them</hi> to take this method. <hi type="italic">The word of the</hi> Lord must <hi type="italic">go forth from Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>. And see <reference osisRef="Joel.2.32">Joel ii. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.16">iii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Obad.1.21">Obad. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">Zech. xiv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Because there the matters of fact on which the gospel was founded were transacted; and therefore there they were first attested, where, if there had been any just cause for it, they might be best contested and disproved. So strong, so bright, is the first shining forth of the glory of the risen Redeemer that it dares face those daring enemies of his that had put him to an ignominious death, and sets them at defiance. "<hi type="italic">Begin at Jerusalem,</hi> that the chief priests may try their strength to crush the gospel, and may rage to see themselves disappointed." <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Because he would give us a further example of forgiving enemies. Jerusalem had put the greatest affronts imaginable upon him (both the rulers and the multitude), for which that city might justly have been excepted by name out of the act of indemnity; but no, so far from that, the first offer of gospel grace is made to Jerusalem, and thousands there are in a little time brought to partake of that grace. <div eID="gen26570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26571" type="x-p"/> (3.) What <hi type="italic">assistance they should have in preaching.</hi> It is a vast undertaking that they are here called to, a very large and difficult province, especially considering the opposition this service would meet with, and the sufferings it would be attended with. If therefore they ask, <hi type="italic">Who is sufficient for these things?</hi> here is an answer ready: <hi type="italic">Behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you,</hi> and <hi type="italic">you shall be endued with power from on high,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.49">v. 49</reference>. He here assures them that in a little time the Spirit should be poured out upon them in greater measures than ever, and they should thereby be furnished with all those gifts and graces which were necessary to their discharge of this great trust; and therefore they must <hi type="italic">tarry at Jerusalem,</hi> and not enter upon it till this be done. Note, [1.] Those who <hi type="italic">receive the Holy Ghost</hi> are thereby <hi type="italic">endued with a power from on high,</hi> a supernatural power, a power above any of their own; it is <hi type="italic">from on high,</hi> and therefore draws the soul upward, and makes it to <hi type="italic">aim high.</hi> [2.] Christ's apostles could never have planted his gospel, and set up his kingdom in the world, as they did, if they had not been endued with such a power; and their admirable achievements prove that there was an excellency of power going along with them. [3.] <hi type="italic">This power from on high</hi> was the <hi type="italic">promise of the Father,</hi> the great promise of the New Testament, as the promise of the coming of Christ was of the Old Testament. And, if it be the <hi type="italic">promise of the Father,</hi> we may be sure that the promise is <hi type="italic">inviolable</hi> and the thing promised <hi type="italic">invaluable.</hi> [4.] Christ would not leave his disciples till the time was just at hand for the performing of this promise. It was but ten days after the <hi type="italic">ascension</hi> of Christ that there came the <hi type="italic">descent</hi> of the Spirit. [5.] Christ's ambassadors must stay till they have their powers, and not venture upon their embassy till they have received full instructions and credentials. Though, one would think, never was such haste as now for the preaching of the gospel, yet the preachers must tarry till they be endued with power from on high, and <hi type="italic">tarry at Jerusalem,</hi> though a place of danger, because there this promise of the Father was to find them, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joel ii. 28</reference>.
entries.b919baa26944c8beda3876b07160e71bc3074e0f: <div eID="gen26571" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Ascension.</title> <div sID="gen26572" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">50</hi> And he led them out as far as to Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them. <hi type="super">51</hi> And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven. <hi type="super">52</hi> And they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy: <hi type="super">53</hi> And were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen. <div eID="gen26572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26573" type="x-p"/> This evangelist omits the solemn meeting between Christ and his disciples <hi type="italic">in Galilee;</hi> but what he said to them there, and at other interviews, he subjoins to what he said to them at the first visit he made them on the evening of the day he rose; and has now nothing more to account for but his ascension into heaven, of which we have a very brief narrative in these verses, in which we are told, <div eID="gen26573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26574" type="x-p"/> I. How solemnly Christ took leave of his disciples. Christ's design being to reconcile heaven and earth, and to continue a days-man between them, it was necessary that he should lay his hands on them both, and, in order thereunto, that he should <hi type="italic">pass</hi> and <hi type="italic">repass.</hi> He had business to do in both worlds, and accordingly came from heaven to earth in his incarnation, to despatch his business here, and, having finished this, he returned to heaven, to reside there, and negotiate our affairs with the Father. Observe, 1. Whence he ascended: from <hi type="italic">Bethany,</hi> near Jerusalem, adjoining to the <hi type="italic">mount of Olives.</hi> There he had done eminent services for his Father's glory, and there he entered upon his glory. There was the <hi type="italic">garden</hi> in which his sufferings began, there he was in his agony; and Bethany signifies <hi type="italic">the house of sorrow.</hi> Those that would go to heaven must ascend thither from the house of sufferings and sorrow, must go by agonies to their joys. The mount of Olives was pitched upon long since to be the place of Christ's ascension: <hi type="italic">His feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.14.4">Zech. xiv. 4</reference>. And here it was that awhile ago he began his triumphant entry into Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.22">ch. xix. 29</reference>. 2. Who were the witnesses of his ascension: <hi type="italic">He led out his disciples</hi> to see him. Probably, it was very early in the morning that he ascended, before people were stirring; for he never showed himself openly to all the people after his resurrection, but only to <hi type="italic">chosen witnesses.</hi> The disciples did not see him rise out of the grace, because his resurrection was capable of being proved by their seeing him alive afterwards; but they saw him <hi type="italic">ascend</hi> into heaven, because they could not otherwise have an <hi type="italic">ocular</hi> demonstration of his ascension. They were <hi type="italic">led out</hi> on purpose to see him ascend, had their eye upon him when he ascended, and were not looking another way. 3. What was the farewell he gave them: <hi type="italic">He lifted up his hands, and blessed them.</hi> He did not go away in displeasure, but in love; he left a blessing behind him; <hi type="italic">he lifted up his hands,</hi> as the high priest did when he blessed the people; see <reference osisRef="Lev.9.22">Lev. ix. 22</reference>. He blessed as one having authority, commanded the blessing which he had purchased; he <hi type="italic">blessed them</hi> as Jacob blessed his sons. The apostles were now as the representatives of the twelve tribes, so that in blessing them he blessed all his spiritual Israel, and put his Father's name upon them. He blessed them as Jacob blessed his sons, and Moses the tribes, at parting, to show that, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end. 4. How he left them: <hi type="italic">While he was blessing them, he was parted from them;</hi> not as if he were taken away before he had said all he had to say, but to intimate that his being parted from them did not put an end to his blessing them, for the intercession which he went to heaven to make for all his is a continuation of the blessing. He <hi type="italic">began</hi> to bless them on earth, but he went to heaven to <hi type="italic">go on</hi> with it. Christ was now sending his apostles to preach his gospel to the world, and he gives them his blessing, not for <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> only, but to be conferred in his name upon <hi type="italic">all</hi> that should believe on him through their word; for in him <hi type="italic">all the families of the earth were to be blessed.</hi> 5. How his ascension is described. (1.) He was <hi type="italic">parted from them,</hi> was taken from their head, as Elijah from Elisha's. Note, The dearest friends must part. Those that love us, and pray for us, and instruct us, must be <hi type="italic">parted form us.</hi> The bodily presence of Christ himself was not to be expected always in this world; those that knew him after the flesh must now henceforth know him so no more. (2.) He was <hi type="italic">carried up into heaven;</hi> not by force, but by his own act and deed. As he arose, so he ascended, by his own power, yet attended by angels. There needed no chariot of fire, nor horses of fire; he knew the way, and, being the <hi type="italic">Lord from heaven,</hi> could go back himself. He ascended in a cloud, as the angel in the smoke of Manoah's sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Judg.13.20">Judg. xiii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen26574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26575" type="x-p"/> II. How cheerfully his disciples continued their attendance on him, and on God through him, even now that he was parted from them. 1. They paid their homage to him at his going away, to signify that though he was going into a far country, yet they would continue his loyal subjects, that they were willing to have him reign over them: <hi type="italic">They worshipped him.</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.52">v. 52</reference>. Note, Christ expects <hi type="italic">adoration</hi> from those that receive blessings from him. He <hi type="italic">blessed them,</hi> in token of gratitude for which they <hi type="italic">worshipped him.</hi> This fresh display of Christ's glory drew from them fresh acknowledgments and adorations of it. They knew that though he was <hi type="italic">parted form them,</hi> yet he could, and did, take notice of their adorations of him; the cloud that received him out of their sight did not put them or their services out of his sight. 2. They <hi type="italic">returned to Jerusalem with great joy.</hi> There they were ordered to continue till the Spirit should be poured out upon them, and thither they went accordingly, though it was into the mouth of danger. Thither they went, and there they staid <hi type="italic">with great joy.</hi> This was a wonderful change, and an effect of the opening of their understandings. When Christ told them that he must leave them sorrow filled their hearts; yet now that they see him go they are <hi type="italic">filled with joy,</hi> being convinced at length that it was expedient for them and for the church that he should go away, to send the Comforter. Note, The glory of Christ is the joy, the exceeding joy, of all true believers, even while they are here in this world; much more will it be so when they go to the new Jerusalem, and find him there in his glory. 3. They abounded in acts of devotion while they were in expectation of the promise of the Father, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.53">v. 53</reference>. (1.) They attended the temple-service at the hours of prayer. God had not as yet quite forsaken it, and therefore they did not. <hi type="italic">They were continually in the temple,</hi> as their Master was when he was at Jerusalem. <hi type="italic">The Lord loves the gates of Zion,</hi> and so should we. Some think that they had their place of meeting, as disciples, in some of the chambers of the temple which belonged to some Levite that was <hi type="italic">well affected</hi> to them; but others think it is not likely that this either could be <hi type="italic">concealed from,</hi> or would be <hi type="italic">connived at</hi> by, the chief priests and <hi type="italic">rulers of the temple.</hi> (2.) Temple-sacrifices, they knew, were superseded by Christ's sacrifice, but the temple-songs they joined in. Note, While we are waiting for God's promises we must go forth to meet them with our praises. Praising and blessing God is work that is never out of season: and nothing better prepares the mind for the receiving of the Holy Ghost than holy joy and praise. Fears are silenced, sorrows sweetened and allayed, and hopes kept up. <div eID="gen26575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26576" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">amen</hi> that concludes seems to be added by the church and every believer to the reading of the gospel, signifying an assent to the truths of the gospel, and a hearty concurrence with all the disciples of Christ in praising and blessing God. <hi type="italic">Amen.</hi> Let him be continually praised and blessed.  <chapter eID="Luke.24"/> <div eID="gen26576" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen25082" osisID="Luke" type="book"/>

entries.544465d6673a963fdf1fa7fc2ffb348d4e960a11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14799"/><div sID="gen28564" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14799"/><hi type="bold">14-16. communed and reasoned--</hi>exchanged views and feelings, weighing afresh all the facts, as detailed in <reference osisRef="Luke.24.18-Luke.24.24">Lu 24:18-24</reference>.<div eID="gen28564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drew near--</hi>coming up behind them as from Jerusalem.<div eID="gen28565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyes holden--</hi>Partly He was "in another form" (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.12">Mr 16:12</reference>), and partly there seems to have been an operation on their own vision; though certainly, as they did not believe that He was alive, His company as a fellow traveller was the last thing they would expect, <div eID="gen28566" type="x-p"/>

entries.904e4991aba9471a08f6a03a275045ba7f75fa75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14807"/><div sID="gen28576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14807"/><hi type="bold">28-31. made as though, &c.--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Mark.6.48">Mr 6:48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.3">Ge 18:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.32.24-Gen.32.26">32:24-26</reference>). <div eID="gen28576" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9e16caa635e46c2f9d5eb8da8946e7f21994d73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14810"/><div sID="gen28584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14810"/><hi type="bold">32-34. They now tell each to the other how their hearts burned--</hi>were fired--within them at His talk and His expositions of Scripture. "Ah! <hi type="bold">this accounts for it: We could not understand the glow of self-evidencing light, love, glory that ravished our hearts; but now we do." They cannot rest--</hi>how could they?--they must go straight back and tell the news. They find the eleven, but ere they have time to tell their tale, their ears are saluted with the thrilling news, "The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Simon." Most touching and precious intelligence this. The only one of the Eleven to whom He appeared alone was he, it seems, who had so shamefully denied Him. What passed at that interview we shall never know here. Probably it was too sacred for disclosure. (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.16.7">Mr 16:7</reference>). The two from Emmaus now relate what had happened to them, and while thus comparing notes of their Lord's appearances, lo! Christ Himself stands in the midst of them. What encouragement to doubting, dark, true-hearted disciples! <div eID="gen28584" type="x-p"/>

Jesus ... stood--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="John.20.19">Joh 20:19</reference>). <div eID="gen28585" type="x-p"/>
entries.6edc63022ab25d91e505d8ff202dd285ac3277a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14812"/><div sID="gen28586" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14812"/><hi type="bold">37-38. a spirit--</hi>the ghost of their dead Lord, but not Himself in the body (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.15">Ac 12:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.14.26">Mt 14:26</reference>).<div eID="gen28586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thoughts--</hi>rather, "reasonings"; that is, whether He were risen or no, and whether this was His very self. <div eID="gen28587" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e7ea431d7f3653fd018184b363e95f73b2a4ee7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14813"/><div sID="gen28588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14813"/><hi type="bold">39-43. Behold, &c.--</hi>lovingly offering them both ocular and tangible demonstration of the reality of His resurrection.<div eID="gen28588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a spirit hath not--</hi>an important statement regarding "spirits."<div eID="gen28589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh and bones--</hi>He says not "flesh and blood"; for the blood is the life of the animal and corruptible body (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Ge 9:4</reference>), which "cannot inherit the kingdom of God" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.50">1Co 15:50</reference>); but "flesh and bones," implying the identity, but with diversity of laws, of the resurrection body. (See on <reference osisRef="John.20.24-John.20.28">Joh 20:24-28</reference>). <div eID="gen28590" type="x-p"/>
entries.89b2f045bd911b88c5318ce215ba8fb602f8dbbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14817"/><div sID="gen28594" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14817"/><hi type="bold">44-49. These are the words, &c.--</hi>that is, "Now you will understand what seemed so dark to you when I told you about the Son of man being put to death and rising again" (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.31-Luke.18.34">Lu 18:31-34</reference>).<div eID="gen28594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">while ... yet with you--</hi>a striking expression, implying that He was now, as the dead and risen Saviour, virtually dissevered from this scene of mortality, and from all ordinary intercourse with His mortal disciples.<div eID="gen28595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28596" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">law ... prophets ... psalms--</hi>the three Jewish divisions of the Old Testament Scriptures. <div eID="gen28596" type="x-p"/>
entries.5191f98b083d8a5a18f89867fbc4655b9496628f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14823"/><div sID="gen28604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14823"/><hi type="bold">50-53. to Bethany--</hi>not to the village itself, but on the "descent" to it from Mount Olivet. <div eID="gen28604" type="x-p"/>

entries.6631d16a90bf46e72a285f3d77fd2863e73d5e42: <div eID="gen41223" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen41224" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen41225" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen41225" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen41224" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen41226" type="x-p"/> The women coming early to the sepulchre on the first day of the week, bringing their spices, find the stone rolled away, and the tomb empty, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.1-Luk.24.3">Luk 24:1-3</reference>. They see a vision of angels, who announce Christ's resurrection, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.4-Luk.24.8">Luk 24:4-8</reference>. The women return and tell this to the eleven, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.9">Luk 24:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.10">Luk 24:10</reference>. They believe not, but Peter goes and examines the tomb, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.11">Luk 24:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.12">Luk 24:12</reference>. Christ, unknown, appears to two of the disciples who were going to Emmaus, and converses with them, vv. 13-29. While they are eating together, he makes himself known, and immediately disappears, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.30">Luk 24:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.31">Luk 24:31</reference>. They return to Jerusalem, and announce his resurrection to the rest of the disciples, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.32-Luk.24.35">Luk 24:32-35</reference>. Jesus himself appears to them, and gives them the fullest proof of the reality of his resurrection, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.36-Luk.24.43">Luk 24:36-43</reference>. He preaches to them, and gives them the promise of the Holy Spirit, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.44-Luk.24.49">Luk 24:44-49</reference>. He takes them to Bethany, and ascends to heaven in their sight, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.50">Luk 24:50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.51">Luk 24:51</reference>. They worship him, and return to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.52">Luk 24:52</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.53">Luk 24:53</reference>. <div eID="gen41226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41227" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen41227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41228" type="x-p"/> Bringing the spices - To embalm the body of our Lord: but Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea had done this before the body was laid in the tomb. See <reference osisRef="Joh.19.39">Joh 19:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.40">Joh 19:40</reference>. But there was a second embalming found necessary: the first must have been hastily and imperfectly performed; the spices now brought by the women were intended to complete the preceding operation. <div eID="gen41228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41229" type="x-p"/> And certain others with them - This clause is wanting in BCL, two others; Coptic, Ethiopic, Vulgate, and in all the Itala except two. Dionysius Alexandrinus, and Eusebius also omit it. The omission is approved by Mill, Bengel, Wetstein, Griesbach, and others. Bishop Pearce thinks it should be left out for the following reasons: <div eID="gen41229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41230" type="x-p"/> 1. "They who came to the sepulchre, as is here said, being the same with those who, in <reference osisRef="Luk.23.55">Luk 23:55</reference>, are called the women which came with him from Galilee, there was no room for Luke (I think) to add as here, and some others came with them; because the words in <reference osisRef="Luk.23.55">Luk 23:55</reference>, to which these refer, include all that can be supposed to be designed by the words in question. <div eID="gen41230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41231" type="x-p"/> 2. Luke has named no particular woman here, and therefore he could not add and some others, etc., these words necessarily requiring that the names of the women should have preceded, as is the case in <reference osisRef="Luk.24.10">Luk 24:10</reference>, where, when Mary Magdalene, the other Mary, and Joanna, had been named, it is very rightly added, and other women that were with them."
entries.0c0e54df428ae3522eb46bccff9b391bdda4128c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen41231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41232" type="x-p"/> They found the stone rolled away - An angel from God had done this before they reached the tomb, <reference osisRef="Mat.28.2">Mat 28:2</reference> : On this case we cannot help remarking, that, when persons have strong confidence in God, obstacles do not hinder them from undertaking whatever they have reason to believe he requires; and the removal of them they leave to him: and what is the consequence? They go on their way comfortably, and all difficulties vanish before them.
entries.44469d99e2d5d93c693b4e01be180e1686e84548: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen41232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41233" type="x-p"/> And found not the body of the Lord - His holy soul was in Paradise, <reference osisRef="Luk.23.43">Luk 23:43</reference>; and the evangelist mentions the body particularly, to show that this only was subject to death. It is, I think, evident enough, from these and other words of Luke, that the doctrine of the materiality of the soul, made no part of his creed.
entries.d5254ba2bf89d6ad679d5ebadbfd328525b26b7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen41233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41234" type="x-p"/> Why seek ye the living among the dead? - This was a common form of speech among the Jews, and seems to be applied to those who were foolishly, impertinently, or absurdly employed. As places of burial were unclean, it was not reasonable to suppose that the living should frequent them; or that if any was missing he was likely to be found in such places.
entries.930fc3787179284f441f5f03cd40750d6cd83580: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen41234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41235" type="x-p"/> Sinful men - Or heathens, ανθρωπων ἁμαρτωλων, i.e. the Romans, by whom only he could be put to death; for the Jews themselves acknowledged that this power was now vested in the hands of the Roman governor alone. See <reference osisRef="Joh.19.15">Joh 19:15</reference>.
entries.d6ba1694f7e1ad47fa88b8e3bae31d2c0b53c59d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen41235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41236" type="x-p"/> They remembered his words - Even the simple recollection of the words of Christ becomes often a source of comfort and support to those who are distressed or tempted: for his words are the words of eternal life.
entries.1ae54148e9a45627fcbaf204e9d10f5c42319fee: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen41236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41237" type="x-p"/> And Joanna - She was the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward. See <reference osisRef="Luk.8.3">Luk 8:3</reference>.
entries.e230cc3fcd458a8c8728787b29589a34529cab95: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen41237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41238" type="x-p"/> Then arose Peter - John went with him, and got to the tomb before him. See <reference osisRef="Joh.20.2">Joh 20:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.20.3">Joh 20:3</reference>. <div eID="gen41238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41239" type="x-p"/> The linen clothes laid by themselves - Or, The linen clothes only. This was the fine linen which Joseph of Arimathea bought, and wrapped the body in: <reference osisRef="Mar.15.46">Mar 15:46</reference>. Small as this circumstance may at first view appear, it is, nevertheless, no mean proof of the resurrection of our Lord. Had the body been stolen away, all that was wrapped about it would have been taken away with it; as the delay which must have been occasioned by stripping it might have led to the detection of the theft; nor would the disciples have run such a risk if they had stolen him, when stripping the body could have answered no end. This circumstance is related still more particularly by John, <reference osisRef="Joh.20.5-Joh.20.7">Joh 20:5-7</reference>. Peter seeth the linen clothes lie, and the napkin that was about his head not lying with the linen clothes, but Wrapped together in a place by itself. All these circumstances prove that the thing was done leisurely; order and regularity being observed through the whole. Hurry and confusion necessarily mark every act of robbery.
entries.241b1809a1cef92d46923785e63cff0186a710be: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen41239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41240" type="x-p"/> Behold, two of them - This long and interesting account is not mentioned by Matthew nor John, and is only glanced at by Mark, <reference osisRef="Mar.16.12">Mar 16:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.16.13">Mar 16:13</reference>. One of these disciples was Cleopas, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.18">Luk 24:18</reference>, and the other is supposed by many learned men, both ancient and modern, to have been Luke himself. See the sketch of his life prefixed to these notes. Some of the ancient versions have called the other disciple Ammaus and Ammaon, reading the verse thus: Behold two of them, Ammaus and Cleopas, were going in that very day to a village about sixty furlongs distant from Jerusalem. But the Persian says positively that it was Luke who accompanied Cleopas. See the inscription to section 140 of this Gospel in the Polyglott. Dr. Lightfoot thinks it was Peter, and proves that Cleopas and Alpheus were one and the same person. <div eID="gen41240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41241" type="x-p"/> Threescore furlongs - Some MSS. say 160 furlongs, but this is a mistake; for Josephus assigns the same distance to this village from Jerusalem as the evangelist does. War, b. vii. c. 6. s. 6. Αμμαους απεχει των Ἱεροσολυμων σταδιους ἑξηκοντα, Ammaus is sixty stadia distant from Jerusalem, about seven English miles and three-quarters. A stadium was about 243 yards, according to Arbuthnot.
entries.ee68dfe01c759b204587abb29c144bdb6f8a16bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen41241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41242" type="x-p"/> And reasoned - Συζητειν, concerning the probability or improbability of Christ being the Messiah, or of his resurrection from the dead. It was a laudable custom of the Jews, and very common also, to converse about the law in all their journeyings; and now they had especial reason to discourse together, both of the law and the prophets, from the transactions which had recently taken place.
entries.3ab056ba22f20da882e3971d7d673e6c9c6ed319: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen41242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41243" type="x-p"/> Their eyes were holden - It does not appear that there was any thing supernatural here, for the reason why these persons (who were not apostles, see <reference osisRef="Luk.24.33">Luk 24:33</reference>) did not recollect our Lord is given by Mark, <reference osisRef="Mar.16.12">Mar 16:12</reference>, who says that Christ appeared to them in another form.
entries.c65b0ac50a6b20fa9946f798430436395fb95266: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen41243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41244" type="x-p"/> Cleopas - The same as Alpheus, father of the Apostle James, <reference osisRef="Mar.3.18">Mar 3:18</reference>, and husband of the sister of the virgin. <reference osisRef="Joh.19.25">Joh 19:25</reference>. <div eID="gen41244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41245" type="x-p"/> Art thou only a stranger - As if he had said, What has been done it Jerusalem, within these few days, has been so public, so awful, and so universally known, that, if thou hadst been but a lodger in the city for a single night, I cannot conceive how thou couldst miss hearing of these things: indeed, thou appearest to be the only person unacquainted with them.
entries.7a59ad23c93e801b38e3456f061be5b4de591353: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen41245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41246" type="x-p"/> Which was a prophet - Ανηρ προφητης, a man prophet, a genuine prophet; but this has been considered as a Hebraism: "for, in <reference osisRef="Exo.2.14">Exo 2:14</reference>, a man prince is simply a prince; and in <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.3">1Sam 31:3</reference>, men archers mean no more than archers." But my own opinion is, that this word is often used to deepen the signification, so in the above quotations: Who made thee a man prince (i.e. a mighty sovereign) and a judge over us! <reference osisRef="Exo.2.14">Exo 2:14</reference>. And, the battle went sore against Saul, and the men archers (i.e. the stout, or well aiming archers) hit him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.3">1Sam 31:3</reference>. So in Palaephatus, de Incredib. c. 38. p. 47, quoted by Kypke, ην ανηρ βασιλευς μεγας, He was a great and eminent king. So ανηρ προφητης here signifies, he was a Genuine prophet, nothing like those false ones by whom the people have been so often deceived; and he has proved the divinity of his mission by his heavenly teaching, and astonishing miracles. <div eID="gen41246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41247" type="x-p"/> Mighty in - word - Irresistibly eloquent. Powerful in deed, working incontrovertible miracles. See Kypke in loco.
entries.7a854d2c83df7e66cd39b400f3db7f64d8036d6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen41247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41248" type="x-p"/> Cleopas paints the real state of his own mind in these verses. In his relation there is scarcely any thing well connected; important points are referred to, and not explained, though he considered the person to whom he spoke as entirely unacquainted with these transactions: his own hopes and fears he cannot help mixing with the narration, and throwing over the whole that confusion that dwells in his own heart. The narration is not at all in Luke's style; but as it is probable he was the other disciple who was present, and had heard the words of Cleopas, he gave them in that simple, natural, artless manner in which they were spoken. Had the account been forged, those simple, natural touches would not have appeared. <div eID="gen41248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41249" type="x-p"/> To-day is the third day - Our Lord had often said that he would rise again the third day; and though Alpheus had little hope of this resurrection, yet he could not help recollecting the words he had heard, especially as they seemed to be confirmed by the relation of the women, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.22-Luk.24.24">Luk 24:22-24</reference>.
entries.e80e7b71cc61f033ee8f605663f77681590091fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen41249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41250" type="x-p"/> O fools and slow of heart to believe - Inconsiderate men, justly termed such, because they had not properly attended to the description given of the Messiah by the prophets, nor to his teaching and miracles, as proofs that He alone was the person they described. <div eID="gen41250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41251" type="x-p"/> Slow of heart - Backward, not easy to be persuaded of the truth, always giving way to doubtfulness and distrust. This very imperfection in them is a strong evidence of the truth of the doctrine which they afterwards believed, and proclaimed to the world. Had they not had the fullest assurance of these things, they never would have credited them; and it is no small honor to the new-covenant Scriptures that such persons were chosen, first, to believe them; secondly, to proclaim them in the world; and, thirdly, to die on the evidence of those truths, the blessed influence of which they felt in their own hearts, and fully exemplified in their lives.
entries.4256d23222756fa2870bf4b5b780d4c3934065c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen41251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41252" type="x-p"/> Ought not Christ to have suffered - Ουχι εδει παθειν τον Χριστον, Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer. This was the way in which sin must be expiated, and, without this, no soul could have been saved. The suffering Messiah is he alone by whom Israel and the world can be saved.
entries.d468455ca03c5cb824ec1d60139639d6becb3f69: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen41252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41253" type="x-p"/> Beginning at Moses, etc. - What a sermon this must have been, where all the prophecies relative to the incarnation, birth, teaching, miracles, sufferings, death, and resurrection of the blessed Jesus were all adduced, illustrated, and applied to himself, by an appeal to the well known facts which had taken place during his life! We are almost irresistibly impelled to exclaim, What a pity this discourse had not been preserved! No wonder their hearts burned within them, while hearing such a sermon, from such a preacher. The law and the prophets had all borne testimony, either directly or indirectly, to Christ; and we may naturally suppose that these prophecies and references were those which our Lord at this time explained and applied to himself. See <reference osisRef="Luk.24.32">Luk 24:32</reference>.
entries.fda1be568b2b1ff78cc8a72e58db82eb54d7a1d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen41253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41254" type="x-p"/> He made as though he would have gone farther - That is, he was going on, as though he intended to go farther; and so he doubtless would had they not earnestly pressed him to lodge with them. His preaching had made a deep impression upon their hearts, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.32">Luk 24:32</reference>, and now they feel it their greatest privilege to entertain the preacher. <div eID="gen41254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41255" type="x-p"/> This is a constant effect of the doctrine of Christ: wherever it is felt, the Author of it, the ever-blessed Jesus, is earnestly entreated to dwell in the heart; and he who preaches it, is amply provided with the necessaries of life by those who have received his testimony.
entries.d9e168213dc274c968ce7d9758f8de1fbfa89c90: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen41255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41256" type="x-p"/> For it is toward evening - And consequently both inconvenient and unsafe to proceed to another village. Reader! it is probably the eve of thy life, whether thou be old or young: thy day may have already declined, and there is, possibly, but a step between thee and the eternal world! Hath the Lord Jesus taught thee by his word and Spirit to believe in him, that thou mightest be saved? Is he come into thy heart? Hast thou the witness of his Spirit that thy sin is blotted out through his blood? <reference osisRef="Rom.8.16">Rom 8:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Gal 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.10-1Jn.5.12">1Jn 5:10-12</reference>. If thou have not, get thee to God right humbly. Jesus is about to pass by, perhaps for ever! O, constrain him, by earnest faith and prayer, to enter into thy soul, and lodge with thee! May God open Thy eyes! May he stir up and inflame Thy heart! <div eID="gen41256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41257" type="x-p"/> And he went in - And so he will to thee, thou penitent soul! Therefore take courage, and be not faithless but believing.
entries.082572c8155b186c696f99e71d98371dd0a876b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen41257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41258" type="x-p"/> He took bread - This was the office of the master and father of a family, and this was our Lord's usual custom among his disciples. Those whom Christ lodges with he feeds, and feeds too with bread that himself hath blessed, and this feeding not only strengthens, but also enlightens the soul.
entries.4b054c11b17af5d908c4ca1af635b5d70cbc2701: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen41258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41259" type="x-p"/> Their eyes were opened - But we are not to imagine that he administered the holy eucharist at this time; there is not the most distant evidence of this. It was a mere family meal, and ended before it was well begun. <div eID="gen41259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41260" type="x-p"/> They knew him - His acting as father of the family, in taking, blessing, and distributing the bread among them, caused them to recollect those lips which they had often heard speak, and those hands by which they had often been fed. Perhaps he also threw off the disguise which he had before assumed; and now appeared in his own person. <div eID="gen41260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41261" type="x-p"/> He vanished out of their sight - Probably, during their surprise, he took the opportunity of withdrawing from the place; leaving them to reflect and meditate on what they had heard and seen.
entries.c8108f00fdac4de54c8a33340a68dd42b7b2f92a: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen41261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41262" type="x-p"/> Did not our heart burn within us - His word was in our heart as a burning fire, <reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jer 20:9</reference>. Our hearts waxed hot within us, and while we were musing the fire burned, <reference osisRef="Psa.39.3">Psa 39:3</reference>. In some such way as this the words of the disciples may be understood: but there is a very remarkable reading here in the Codex Bezae; instead of καιομενη, burned, it has κεκαλυμμενη, veiled; and one of the Itala has, fuit excaecatum, was blinded. Was not our heart veiled (blinded) when he conversed with us on the way, and while he unfolded the Scriptures to us, seeing we did not know him?
entries.66881abafb104efac740db73345d86cce92a7aba: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen41262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41263" type="x-p"/> Saying, The Lord is risen indeed - The meaning here is, that these two disciples found the apostles, and those who were with them, unanimously testifying that Christ had risen from the dead. It is not the two disciples to whom we are to refer the word λεγοντας, saying; but to the body of the disciples. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mar.16.12">Mar 16:12</reference>.
entries.3f82b7184c6a5a48350ac7549b8e78a9b5458b87: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen41263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41264" type="x-p"/> And they - The two disciples who were just come from Emmaus, related what had happened to them on the way, going to Emmaus, and how he had been known unto them in the breaking of bread, while supping together at the above village. See on <reference osisRef="Luk.24.31">Luk 24:31</reference> (note).
entries.b72034932e0d7663ffffc234a53a8f75f32f2349: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen41264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41265" type="x-p"/> And as they thus spake - While the two disciples who were going to Emmaus were conversing about Christ, he joined himself to their company. Now, while they and the apostles are confirming each other in their belief of his resurrection, Jesus comes in, to remove every doubt, and to give them the fullest evidence of it. And it is ever true that, wherever two or three are gathered together in his name, he is in the midst of them. <div eID="gen41265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41266" type="x-p"/> Peace be unto you - The usual salutation among the Jews. May you prosper in body and soul, and enjoy every heavenly and earthly good! See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.5.9">Mat 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.10.12">Mat 10:12</reference>.
entries.9ba6925b132265c5b88e5737803e631e4a9f32d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen41266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41267" type="x-p"/> And supposed that they had seen a spirit - But if there be no such thing as a disembodied spirit, would not our Lord have shown them their error? Instead of this, he confirms them in their opinion, by saying, A spirit hath not flesh and bones as you see me have, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.39">Luk 24:39</reference>; therefore he says, handle me and see me. They probably imagined that it was the soul only of our blessed Lord which they saw; but they were soon fully convinced of the identity of his person, and the reality of his resurrection; for, <div eID="gen41267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41268" type="x-p"/> 1. They saw his body. <div eID="gen41268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41269" type="x-p"/> 2. They heard him speak. <div eID="gen41269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41270" type="x-p"/> 3. They handled him. <div eID="gen41270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41271" type="x-p"/> 4. They saw him eat a piece of broiled fish and honeycomb, which they gave him. <div eID="gen41271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41272" type="x-p"/> In these things it was impossible for them to have been deceived.
entries.12497117e8f4010b8e4a73d6b44c4e52dd088679: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen41272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41273" type="x-p"/> They - believed not for joy - They were so overcome with the joy of his resurrection, that they did not, for some time, properly receive the evidence that was before them - as we phrase it, they thought the news too good to be true.
entries.e4f90b2c6d4a2766e0ec04d87143e40067ef1f98: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen41273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41274" type="x-p"/> The law - the prophets - the psalms - This was the Jewish division of the whole old covenant. The Law contained the five books of Moses; the Prophets, the Jews divided into former and latter; they were, according to Josephus, thirteen. "The Psalms included not only the book still so named, but also three other books, Proverbs, Job, and Canticles. <div eID="gen41274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41275" type="x-p"/> These all," says the above author, "contain hymns to God, and rules for the conduct of the lives of men." Joseph. Cont. App. i. 8. This account is imperfect: the common Jewish division of the writings of the old covenant is the following, and indeed seems to be the same to which our Lord alludes: - <div eID="gen41275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41276" type="x-p"/> I. The Law, תורה thorah, including Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. <div eID="gen41276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41277" type="x-p"/> II. The Prophets, נביאים, nabiaim, or teachers, including Joshua, Judges, the two books of Samuel, and the two books of Kings: these were termed the former prophets. Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi: these were termed the latter prophets. <div eID="gen41277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41278" type="x-p"/> III. The Hagiographa, (holy writings), כתובים kethuvim, which comprehended the Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Canticles, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and the two books of Chronicles. The Jews made anciently only twenty-two books of the whole, to bring them to the number of the letters in the Hebrew alphabet; and this they did by joining Ruth to Judges, making the two books of Samuel only one; and so of Kings and Chronicles; joining the Lamentations to Jeremiah, and making the twelve minor prophets only one book.
entries.27a294052173860b069dbdad73bc45ff5360cc1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen41278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41279" type="x-p"/> Then opened he their understanding - Διηνοιξεν, He fully opened. They had a measure of light before, so that they discerned the Scriptures to be the true word of God, and to speak of the Messiah; but they had not light sufficient to enable them to apply these Scriptures to their Lord and Master; but now, by the influence of Christ, they see, not only, the prophecies which pointed out the Messiah, but also the Messiah who was pointed out by these prophecies. The book of God may be received in general as a Divine revelation, but the proper meaning, reference, and application of the Scriptures can only be discerned by the light of Christ. Even the very plain word of God is a dead letter to those who are not enlightened by the grace of Christ; and why? because this word speaks of spiritual and heavenly things; and the carnal mind of man cannot discern them. They who receive not this inward teaching continue dark and dead while they live.
entries.ec35580b296b3af1ca6a00e2c3bebb4fea378bc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen41279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41280" type="x-p"/> Repentance - See its nature fully explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.1">Mat 3:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen41280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41281" type="x-p"/> Remission of sins - Αφεσιν ἁμαρτιων, The taking away - removal of sins, in general every thing that relates to the destruction of the power, the pardoning of the guilt, and the purification of the heart from the very nature of sin. <div eID="gen41281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41282" type="x-p"/> Should be preached in his name - See the office of a proclaimer, herald, or preacher, explained in the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.1">Mat 3:1</reference> (note), and particularly at the end of that chapter. <div eID="gen41282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41283" type="x-p"/> In his name - On his authority, and in virtue of the atonement made by him: for on what other ground could the inhabitants of the earth expect remission of sins? <div eID="gen41283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41284" type="x-p"/> Among all nations - Because God wills the salvation of All; and Jesus Christ by his grace has tasted death for Every man. <reference osisRef="Heb.2.9">Heb 2:9</reference>. <div eID="gen41284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41285" type="x-p"/> Beginning at Jerusalem - Making the first overtures of mercy to my murderers! If, then, the sinners of Jerusalem might repent, believe, and be saved, none, on this side hell, need despair.
entries.dccc3a5a0734c66e9c54ddbf1c50a1c1d3eb8def: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen41285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41286" type="x-p"/> Ye are witnesses of these things - He gave them a full commission to proclaim these glad tidings of peace and salvation to a lost world. The disciples were witnesses not only that Christ had suffered and rose again from the dead; but also that he opens the understanding by the inspiration of his Spirit, that he gives repentance, that he pardons sin, and purifies from all unrighteousness, and that he is not willing that any should perish, but that all should come unto the knowledge of the truth and be saved. And these are the things of which their successors in the Gospel ministry must bear witness. As far as a man steadily and affectionately proclaims these doctrines, so far God will bless his labor to the salvation of those who hear him. But no man can with any propriety bear witness of that grace that saves the soul, whose own soul is not saved by that grace.
entries.1b2dfb50e442321266dfbe753e8c8eb89f4ef8c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 49</hi> <div eID="gen41286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41287" type="x-p"/> The promise of my Father - That is, the Holy Ghost, promised, <reference osisRef="Joh.15.26">Joh 15:26</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Act.1.4">Act 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.2.33">Act 2:33</reference>. <div eID="gen41287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41288" type="x-p"/> Until ye be endued with power - The energy of the Holy Ghost was to be communicated to them for three particular purposes. <div eID="gen41288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41289" type="x-p"/> 1. That he might be in them, a sanctifying comforter, fortifying their souls and bringing to their remembrance whatever Jesus had before spoken to them. <div eID="gen41289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41290" type="x-p"/> 2. That their preaching might be accompanied by his demonstration and power to the hearts of their hearers, so that they might believe and be saved. <div eID="gen41290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41291" type="x-p"/> 3. That they might be able to work miracles to confirm their pretensions to a Divine mission, and to establish the truth of the doctrines they preached.
entries.85ac3a539cd38e1f413bbd3cdf08ed91dc9099d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 50</hi> <div eID="gen41291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41292" type="x-p"/> He led them out as far as to Bethany - The difficulties in this verse, when collated with the accounts given by the other evangelists, are thus reconciled by Dr. Lightfoot. "I. This very evangelist (<reference osisRef="Act.1.12">Act 1:12</reference>) tells us, that when the disciples came back from the place where our Lord had ascended, they returned from mount Olivet, distant from Jerusalem a Sabbath day's journey. But now the town of Bethany was about fifteen furlongs from Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Joh.11.18">Joh 11:18</reference>, and that is double a Sabbath day's journey. "II. Josephus tells us that mount Olivet was but five furlongs from the city, and a Sabbath day's journey was seven furlongs and a half. Antiq. lib. 20, cap. 6. About that time there came to Jerusalem a certain Egyptian, pretending himself a prophet, and persuading the people that they should go out with him to the mount of Olives, Ὁ και της πολεως αντικρυς κειμενον, απεχει σταδια πεντε; which, being situated on the front of the city, is distant five furlongs. These things are all true: <div eID="gen41292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41293" type="x-p"/> 1. That the mount of Olives lay but five furlongs distant from Jerusalem. <div eID="gen41293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41294" type="x-p"/> 2. That the town of Bethany was fifteen furlongs. <div eID="gen41294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41295" type="x-p"/> 3. That the disciples were brought by Christ as far as Bethany. <div eID="gen41295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41296" type="x-p"/> 4. That, when they returned from the mount of Olives, they traveled more than five furlongs. And, <div eID="gen41296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41297" type="x-p"/> 5. Returning from Bethany, they traveled but a Sabbath day's journey. All which may be easily reconciled, if we would observe: - That the first space from the city was called Bethphage, which I have cleared elsewhere from Talmudic authors, the evangelists themselves also confirming it. That part of that mount was known by that name to the length of about a Sabbath day's journey, till it came to that part which is called Bethany. For there was a Bethany, a tract of the mount, and the town of Bethany. The town was distant from the city about fifteen furlongs, i.e. about two miles, or a double Sabbath day's journey: but the first border of this tract (which also bore the name of Bethany) was distant but one mile, or a single Sabbath day's journey. "Our Savior led out his disciples, when he was about to ascend, to the very first region or tract of mount Olivet, which was called Bethany, and was distant from the city a Sabbath day's journey. And so far from the city itself did that tract extend itself which was called Bethphage; and when he was come to that place where the bounds of Bethphage and Bethany met and touched one another, he then ascended; in that very place where he got upon the ass when he rode into Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Mar.11.1">Mar 11:1</reference>. Whereas, therefore, Josephus saith that mount Olivet was but five furlongs from the city, he means the first brink and border of it. But our evangelist must be understood of the place where Christ ascended, where the name of Olivet began, as it was distinguished from Bethphage." <div eID="gen41297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41298" type="x-p"/> Between the appearance of Christ to his apostles, mentioned in <reference osisRef="Luk.24.36">Luk 24:36</reference>, etc., almost all the forty days had passed, before he led them out to Bethany. They went by his order into Galilee, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.32">Mat 26:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.28.10">Mat 28:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.14.28">Mar 14:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.16.7">Mar 16:7</reference>; and there he appeared to them, as is mentioned by Matthew, <reference osisRef="Mat.28.16">Mat 28:16</reference>, etc., and more particularly by John, <reference osisRef="Joh.21.1">Joh 21:1</reference>, etc. See Bishop Pearce. <div eID="gen41298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41299" type="x-p"/> Lifted up his hands - Probably to lay them on their heads, for this was the ordinary way in which the paternal blessing was conveyed, See <reference osisRef="Gen.48.8-Gen.48.20">Gen 48:8-20</reference>.
entries.cf22c2de20fc410fb23bcab63e4f1b774b8215ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 51</hi> <div eID="gen41299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41300" type="x-p"/> Carried up into heaven - Ανεφερετο - into that heaven from which he had descended, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.3.13">Joh 3:13</reference>. This was forty days after his resurrection, <reference osisRef="Act.1.3">Act 1:3</reference>, during which time he had given the most convincing proofs of that resurrection, not only to the apostles, but to many others - to upwards of five hundred at one time, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.6">1Cor 15:6</reference>. <div eID="gen41300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41301" type="x-p"/> As in his life they had seen the way to the kingdom, and in his death the price of the kingdom, so in his ascension they had the fullest proof of the immortality of the soul, the resurrection of the human body, and of his continual intercession at the right hand of God. <div eID="gen41301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41302" type="x-p"/> There are some remarkable circumstances relative to this ascension mentioned in <reference osisRef="Act.1.4-Act.1.12">Act 1:4-12</reference>.
entries.3d92f8d4dbea62a144d553063f4e3b3bafbd9361: <hi type="bold">Verse 52</hi> <div eID="gen41302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41303" type="x-p"/> They worshipped him - Let it be observed that this worship was not given by way of civil respect, for it was after he was parted from them, and carried back into heaven, that they offered it to him; but acts of civil respect are always performed in the presence of the person. They adored him as their God, and were certainly too much enlightened to be capable of any species of idolatry. <div eID="gen41303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41304" type="x-p"/> Returned to Jerusalem with great joy - Having the fullest proof that Jesus was the promised Messiah; and that they had a full commission to preach repentance and remission of sin to mankind, and that they should be Divinely qualified for this great work by receiving the promise of the Father, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.49">Luk 24:49</reference>.
entries.61f302959df2ac4b1f54e9debd6e207f7e1e9c37: <hi type="bold">Verse 53</hi> <div eID="gen41304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41305" type="x-p"/> Were continually in the temple - Especially till the day of pentecost came, when they received the promise, mentioned <reference osisRef="Luk.24.49">Luk 24:49</reference>. <div eID="gen41305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41306" type="x-p"/> Praising and blessing God - Magnifying his mercy, and speaking good of his name. Thus the days of their mourning were ended; and they began that life upon earth in which they still live in the kingdom of God. May the God of infinite love give the reader the same portion in time and in eternity, through the same glorious and ever-blessed Jesus! Amen and amen. <div eID="gen41306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41307" type="x-p"/> There are various subscriptions to this book in the MSS. and versions. The following are the principal. <div eID="gen41307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41308" type="x-p"/> Through the assistance of the Most High God, the Gospel of St. Luke the physician, the proclaimer of eternal life, is finished. Arab. - The most holy Gospel of Luke the Evangelist is completed. Syr. - The end of the holy Gospel according to Luke - written in Greek - published in Alexandria the Great, - in Troas, - in Rome, - in the confines of Achaia and Baeotia, - in Bithynia, - in Macedonia, - in the Italic (or Latin) character, fifteen years after the ascension of Christ. <div eID="gen41308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41309" type="x-p"/> It is likely, the word Amen was added by the Church, on the reading of this book; but there is no evidence that it was affixed by the evangelist. It is omitted by some of the best MSS. and versions. <div eID="gen41309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41310" type="x-p"/> It is evident that, at the conclusion of this Gospel, St. Luke passes very rapidly over a number of interesting circumstances related by the other evangelists, and particularly by St. John, concerning the last forty days of our Lord's sojourning on earth; but, to compensate for this, he has mentioned a variety of important particulars which the others have passed by, a list of which I think it necessary to subjoin. It seems as if the providence of God had designed that none of these evangelists should stand alone: each has his peculiar excellence, and each his own style and mode of narration. They are all witnesses to the truth in general; and each most pointedly to every great fact of the Gospel history. In each there is something new; and no serious reader ever finds that the perusal of any one supersedes the necessity of carefully consulting and reading the others. The same facts and doctrines are exhibited by all in different points of view, which renders them both impressive and interesting; and this one circumstance serves to fix the narrative more firmly in the memory. We should have had slighter impressions from the Gospel history, had we not had the narrative at four different hands. This variety is of great service to the Church of God, and has contributed very much to diffuse the knowledge of the facts and doctrines contained in this history. Parallel passages have been carefully studied, and the different shades of meaning accurately marked out; and the consequence has been, what the wisdom of God designed, the fuller edification of the faithful. It is not the business of a commentator to point out beauties in the composition of the sacred text. Many might be selected from the evangelists in general, and not a few from Luke, who not only tells a true story, but tells it well; especially when he has occasion to connect the different parts of the narration with observations of his own. But this is his least praise: from his own account we learn that he took the utmost pains to get the most accurate and circumstantial information relative to the facts he was to relate: see the note on <reference osisRef="Luk.1.3">Luk 1:3</reference>. While, therefore, he thus diligently and conscientiously sought for truth, the unerring Spirit of God led him into all truth. Even he who expected the revelation of the Almighty, and to be inspired by the Holy Spirit, that he might correctly, forcibly, and successfully proclaim the truth and righteousness of his Maker, must stand upon his watch, and set himself upon his tower, and watch to see what God would speak In him, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab 2:1</reference>. In a similar spirit we may expect the fruits of these revelations. He who carefully and conscientiously uses the means may expect the accomplishment of the end. <div eID="gen41310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41311" type="x-p"/> I cannot close these observations with a more profitable word than what is contained in that truly apostolic and sublime prayer for the second Sunday in Advent; and may he who reads it weigh every word in the spirit of faith and devotion! "Blessed God! who hast caused all holy scriptures to be written for our learning; grant that we may in such wise hear them, read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest them, that, by patience and comfort of thy holy word, we may embrace and ever hold fast the blessed hope of everlasting life, which thou hast given us in our Savior Jesus Christ!" <div eID="gen41311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41312" type="x-p"/> Now to him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood, and hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father, to Him be glory and dominion for ever and ever! Amen.  <chapter eID="Luke.24"/> <div eID="gen41312" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen39738" osisID="Luke" type="book"/>
